**Lessons, admonitions and reflections**

When envy took hold of the hearts of Joseph's brothers (peace be upon him), He showed the wronged one the fate of the wrongdoer in a mirror: ﴿Indeed, I saw eleven stars﴾.

Your gratitude does not equal the measure of your strength.

A beast that does not work for its fodder is no beast at all.

Whenever you see the intellect preferring the perishable over the everlasting, know that it has been transformed (musukh).

Whenever you see that the love of God and readiness to meet Him have departed from the heart, and that love of the created and contentment with, and comfort in, the life of this world have settled in it, know that it has been swallowed up (khusf).

Whenever the eye runs dry of weeping out of fear of God Most High, know that its dryness comes from the hardness of the heart, and the hardest of hearts is the furthest from God.

Whenever you see yourself fleeing from intimacy with Him to intimacy with creatures, and from solitude with God to solitude with other things, know that you are not fit for Him.

Whenever you see Him increasing others while you do not seek more, and bringing others near while you do not draw close, then if a foot moves toward visiting Him while your heart stays behind at home, know that this is a veil and a punishment. The temperament of faith has deviated from soundness, and the pulse of desire beats violently.

If the humours of appetites dominate the limbs of laziness, they are restrained from movement, and various diseases are produced. Yet a purgative is not easy for you to drink. If you remedy the illness, well; otherwise it will kill you.

Had you protected yourself for one hour, you would not need treatment with medicine for a long period.

Whoever mounts the back of neglect and idleness will be brought down into the house of hardship and regret.

Your Lord loves the life of your soul while you want to kill it. He wants ease for you while you want hardship. He wants honour for it while you strive to humiliate it:

*What can an enemy do to a fool
that the fool cannot do to himself?*

Whoever travels by night through the darkness upon the swift camels of patience reaches the dawn of the abode of joy. Whoever sleeps on the bed of laziness wakes up cast into the valley of regret. Diligence is all movement, and laziness is all stillness. Your slackness in striving for virtues is a sign of the feminisation of resolve.

If you want to know the rooster from the hen at the time it emerges from the egg, hang it by its beak: if it moves, it is a rooster; otherwise, it is a hen.

The world is like a prostitute who does not remain faithful to one husband; therefore her lovers are blamed.

*She displayed her beauty and her deeds,
and then the comeliness proved to be ugliness, and did not hold.*

*She swore to us that she would not break her pledges,
as if she had sworn to us that she would not keep them.*

A dinar does not receive the stamp of the king's name until its ingot has endured being repeatedly put into the fire, which removes all its impurity; then it endures being cut into dinars; then it endures being struck upon the die, and only then does the imprint of the design appear upon it. How then can one hope for the design to be imprinted upon hearts in which faith has been written when they are entirely impure? The hardship of the desert is made light by remembering the House (of God), which is reached through the valley of hunger and the valley of sleeplessness, until the landmarks of the abode come into view.

When the riding camels lag in their journey, let the drivers' songs of encouragement rise around them, and the night journey will become pleasant for them.

When the clouds of desire come between hearts and the sun of guidance, the wayfarer is bewildered.

The brute animal considers the consequences, while you see only the present.

You hardly concern yourself with provision for winter before the cold grows strong, nor with provision for summer before the heat grows strong, yet the ant stores up its food in summer for the days of winter.

And this bird, when it knows that its mate has conceived, begins to carry twigs to build the nest before laying. Do you not know that your departure to the grave is near? Why then do you not send ahead a bed (for yourself)? ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for their own souls that they prepare﴾.

And this jerboa does not make a burrow except in firm ground, so that it is safe from the wind; it makes it high so that it is safe from floods; it makes it beside a sand-hill or a rock so that it does not lose its way. Then it makes several entrances, thinning some of them so that they can be broken through if needed. When an enemy comes through an open entrance, it pushes with its head through the thin earth and escapes. But you have tightened the noose around your own self and left no place for escape.

The soul is like an enemy: if it knows that your earnestness is sincere, it submits to you; if it forgets your disgrace, it takes you captive. If you deprive it of the delights of what is permitted, peace will be concluded upon abstaining from what is forbidden. But when you need to seek what is permitted, then it is either a favour bestowed or a ransom paid.

The world and Satan are two enemies outside you, while the soul is an enemy between your two sides.

From the sunnah of jihad: ﴿Fight those of the disbelievers who are near you﴾.

Is not the one who is ready to be struck like an ambush which appears upon you from where you do not perceive?

The least that the soul does to you is to tear your life apart with the hand of squandering and idleness. Take it into the house of reflection for an hour, then consider whether it is with you or against you, and treat it according to whichever of the two it proves to be.

Whoever the world does not weep over, the Hereafter will not smile upon.

The cloud of weariness will clear away at the dawn of the Hereafter. How many a patient one has refrained from desire until he heard, "Eat, O you who did not eat!" O you who envied the one who lowered the veil of blessings upon the dome, and gave him to us until he reached the measure of "Indeed, We found him patient."

How can one prosper who complains to his Lord of the night because of the length of his day, and of the day because of his own ugly deeds? How can one prosper who is a carcass by night and a bustling gadfly by day, who sets up (his scales) with the balance of fraud and the measure of cheating, while destiny is the third of the three stones (of the cooking pot)?

If the bird thought about slaughter, it would not circle around the wheat. Had the horses not endured patiently the scarcity of fodder, they would not have been called the "swift ones".

*Among the harms done to the people of love is that they fell in love without knowing the world or understanding it.*

*Their souls perish from longing, and their eyes (perish) in pursuit of every ugly thing whose face is beautiful.*

*Let your camel-litter carry every fair one; for each of them is today a trusted keeper.*

*What is in your litters is no recompense for my soul, if I die of longing; nor is there in them any price for her.*

*I stayed awake after your departure out of loneliness for you, then my bitterness continued and sleep was restrained.*

*Do not meet your age except unconcerned, as long as your spirit remains accompanied by the body.*

*What lasts in joy in which you rejoiced? The absent one's sorrow does not return to you.*

If you are not among the helpers of the Messenger, then take up war; and if you do not, then be among the guards of the tents; and if you do not, then be among the onlookers of the war who wish for victory for the Muslims. Do not become the fourth, lest you perish. If you see the door shut in your face, be content to stand outside the house, facing the door, asking and seeking, perhaps (it will open). But do not turn your back and say, "What can I do, since the door has been closed to me?"

When the caller of bounties called out, ﴿Whoever brings a good deed, for him is ten times its like﴾, the swift camels of deeds set out. Then the recompense rose, calling to the guide, ﴿And had We not strengthened you﴾, and he said, "None of you will be saved by his deeds."

If you cannot reach the watering-places of the people of resolve, then take the remaining pools. Whoever does not have a son of a male camel, will accept from him a female camel in its second year.

Do not belittle a sin, for how many a spark has set fire (to a whole field)!

Do you not know the secret of ﴿And do not approach this tree﴾? Had Adam been content, he would have been satisfied, but the trial lay in the greed. Solitude is a snare for the hunting of intimacy. The most concealed of hunters is the one who is least in motion, and the most successful at catching game. The hunter does not make a sound.

*Forever the souls of lovers
yearn for your abodes;
and likewise hearts, through remembrance of you,
after fear, find rest.*

And another said:

*Of my ruins, when the lovesick one complains to them,
he complains to one without speech, to one without understanding.*

And another said:

*The life of a young man is only a caravan for him;
from it he returns either a winner or a loser.*

Another said:

*You are startled when funerals meet us,
and we play when they pass by in haste.*

*Like the fright of a flock at the appearance of a wolf,
which, when it disappears, they return to grazing.*

Take your soul with resolution and do not seek concessions. The wall of the inner self is in ruins, so why plaster it? Knowledge and action are twins whose mother is loftiness of aspiration. Ignorance and idleness are twins whose mother is preferring laziness.

O teacher, be steadfast with the beginner, and be measured in private, for the scholar has firmness and the learner has restlessness.

And O seeker, be humble in seeking, for the dust between us is under the sole of the foot; it became a purifier for the face.

The bride of knowledge has been unveiled to you, but she is not a suitable match for you. Looking is permitted only when the contract is valid.

﴿So lower your gaze, for you are of the tribe of Numayr﴾.

The scholar is not a single person; the scholar is the one of writings. The scholar's children are those who live on in his writings, not merely his offspring.

Whoever is created for knowledge shows his essence from childhood. Long wakefulness leads to a pleasant bed, while humiliation lurks in the shade of ease. The greatness of perils lies in riding perils.

The waters of meanings are stored in the heart of the scholar; from it he opens channels for irrigation, one flow after another, and keeps the purest for the people of purity. When they multiply upon him, he calls out to the path, so his knowledge remains flowing, and therefore the zakat of gratitude is multiplied upon him. Every time, the merchandise of his thought travels from the city of his heart to the hearts of seekers; his tongue's broker calls it out, and he displays it in the seasons of counsel to the merchants of pursuit and resolve, (asking) who will buy his wisdom and knowledge at a chosen price.

So O you who sees the height of that rank, do not forget the steps.

How many have crossed a salty sea until they reached sweet water! How many have wandered in a barren desert until they were named "the guide"! How many have worn out the vehicles of the body, cracked open the desires of the senses, travelled by night and day without rest, and kindled the fire of patience in the darkness of desire! If you trust his trustworthiness, then this is the account of the journey.

The world hurls its arrows at its children and says, "Take your precautions," for this reason the blood of its slain is wasted.

The hoopoe was absent from Solomon for a while, and he threatened it. O you who have prolonged your absence from your Lord, have you felt safe from His wrath?

The three who stayed behind from the Messenger ﷺ in one expedition suffered what you have heard. How then will it be for one whose whole life is spent staying behind from him?

When the crow becomes drunk with the wine of greed, it moves about among carrion; but when it sobers from its intoxication, it regrets the ruins. Moses opposed al-Khidr three times on the path of companionship, and then (al-Khidr) untied the knot of union with the hand of, "This is the parting between me and you." Do you not fear, O you who never once kept faith with his Lord, that in some of your slips you will say, "This is the parting between me and you"? The greatest punishment of the people of Hell is their ignorance of the One who punishes.

If their knowledge of what Malik (the keeper of Hell) possessed were correct, they would not have cried out to Malik, "O Malik!"

A person who was not of their kind fell among them, possessing within himself a particle of knowledge; so whenever the Fire was driven against him, he warded it off with a shield, (calling), "O Merciful! O Bestower!"

His death in sins was a resting-place, and then (he was) a grave in Hell; when the spirit stirred within him, he was brought out from the grave.

The sparrow's greed strangles it, and the spider, content in a corner of weakness, has flies driven to it as its food. Many a striver is (outdone) by one who sits still.

You sent your heart after every object of desire, and then you send after it at the time of prayer, but perhaps the messenger will not reach it, so you pray without a heart.

*You left your heart among the longings when you alighted
at al-Mazimayn, on the morning of the departure, with the stop.*

*And you went seeking in the land of Iraq in the forenoon
what was lost at Mina; so wonder at this report.*

*When we came to Mina, the heart was with me,
but it went astray from me between the lost and the spear-thrusts.*

*By the feet of the camels the sands will inform you; I walk in my passion only upon their tracks.*

O you who has lost his heart, do not despair of its return.

*Perhaps God will bring together two scattered ones after
they thought with the fullest thought that they would never meet.*

Desire is a resident, and right judgment is a passer-by; expelling the resident is difficult, and holding onto the passer-by is harder.

You have not ceased to be in prison. The first prison is the loins of the father; the second is the belly of the mother; the third is the swaddling clothes and the cradle; the fourth is the school; the fifth is toil for dependants; the sixth is the illness of death; the seventh is the grave. If you fall into the eighth, you will forget the bitterness of every prison that came before.

Enter the prison of piety by your own choice for some days, so that release may be yours permanently. Do not prefer the release of your soul in what you love, for that brings the prison of eternity.

Blame upon one bearing love is an addition, like Mirrikh (Mars) to the pole of the Pleiades; it finds it, so a report of torment is narrated to it. Thus, when you have left sin but have not undone the knot of persistence, it benefits nothing, just as if an illness subsides without purging: it remains in its state. If the intention of the heart is not realised, speech has no effect.

The oath of one compelled is not binding. Woe to you! Your soul is your merchandise, and the buyer has bid for it at the finest price; so strive to correct its faults, so that it may be pleasing to Him to whom it is sold.

The dreams of wishes are confused dreams; the guide of hopes is a liar; the pasture of desires is a dire place. Impotence is the partner of deprivation; negligence and laziness are calamities.

Your heart's lock is Byzantine; no trickery can reach it.

Whenever one of the soldiers of your resolve betrays you, your heart cannot feel safe from defeat through him.

When there is a flaw in the pipes, the wind goes into the heads of the reeds. You are a guardian over your limbs and your subjects; when you have given them their portions, then demand their rights from them.

Reflect upon His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, so that you will be miserable﴾. Observe how He associated the two in the expulsion, and singled out the male for misery, because he is occupied with earning and livelihood, while the woman is secluded in her curtained place.

*Take from the pure water provision; for in the valley of al-Ghada
you will find no fresh water nor any coolness.*

*Is there any breath of the ben-tree and the myrtle? Far-fetched is a valley that grows ben and myrtle!*

*Turn your eye toward Najd; for when you travel,
you will not see Aqiq nor Najd.*

Look to the right, and see whether you see a trial; then turn to the left, and see whether you see only regret. As for the inhabited abode, it has become a ruin; as for the captivity of death, it is a planting; as for the rider, the horse has thrown him down. They travelled in a darkness of their own wrongdoing, with no torch in hand. The ships of their salvation stood still, because the sea had dried up. All those dwellings turned upside down into misfortune. Munkar came with the last of the (day), and Nakir with the first of the frowning. Will not one who has long been sitting arise for his salvation?

*O soul, this is nothing but the patience of days,
whose span seems like the dreams of sleep.*

*O soul, withdraw from this world and its pleasures,
and leave it, for life lies ahead of me.*

Will not the bird of passion be patient for a grain whose outcome is unknown? It is only an hour, and then it reaches the tower of safety, and in it there are many grains.

*And if you yearn for the sanctuary and a garden,
then with the ghada there is water and other gardens.*

A bird carrying letters has stronger resolve, so perhaps your placement is not in balance.

The pure spirit is only in a balanced body, and lofty aspiration is only in a noble soul.

When the bird carries the message, it patiently bears its resolve and keeps to the valleys. If the path is hidden from it, it senses the winds and glimpses the disc of the sun, and it is guided. Even in great hunger, it avoids grain thrown down out of fear of a hidden snare, which would entangle its wing and lose what it carries. When it delivers the message, it releases itself to its desires inside the tower.

O bearers of the books of trust, most of you are off the road!

Among you, there is none who is guided by one who has been enchanted by love and descended with what he carried, and then becomes ensnared, his wing entangled, and waits for slaughter. So neither was the grain obtained, nor was the message delivered.

*A dove whom a snare deceived, and she spent the night
pulling at it, her wing caught.*

*Neither at night did she attain what she wished,
nor at dawn was there any release for her.*

Had you patiently endured the hardship of the road, the journey would have ended, and you would have settled, at rest, in the Gardens of Eden. O you who neglect to consider consequences: buy in advance in the time of cheapness, for the change of prices is not safe. Do not hurl the arrows of a glance, for by God they will fall upon you. Many a shepherd has neglected his eye, and so the grazing was raided.

*Every calamity has its beginning in a glance,
and most of the fire comes from a spark that was thought small.*

*How many a glance has done to the heart of its beholder
what arrows do, without bow or string!*

And another said:

*I see that arrows, when the one who shoots them sleeps, are of what use, then, if the arrow strikes the target and is spent?*

Recognise the measure of His kindness, and His preserving you. He forbade you from sins only as protection and safeguard for you, not out of stinginess towards you; and He commanded you to obey out of mercy and benevolence. He has no need of you. Because the intellect knows it, He forbade what would remove it, which is wine, to preserve the house of knowledge. O you who take intoxicants, do not do so: the intoxication of your ignorance is enough for you, so do not combine two intoxications. A commodity—"Indeed I am most forgiving"—is given only at a price, for the one who repents. O you who has departed from the path, and has been secure from the road, and has done righteous deeds: whoever has been struck and then guided, if you cannot strive in deed, then stand at the door of seeking. Expose yourself to a breath of the breaths of the Lord, for in a single moment the one who was far is made successful.

*Do not despair over any calamity that has befallen you,
nor let the enemies see anything to gloat over.*

*And be patient, for by patience the desired is attained;
when you meet a company, stand firm.*

The price of lofty things is diligence; slackness is a disease more bitter than consolation. Are there signs and traces in your eyes? If the heart has grown cold, then fire cannot warm it. Existence is a sea, the scholars are its jewels, the ascetics its ambergris, the merchants its whales, the wicked its crocodiles, and the ignorant upon its surface are like foam. Were the world to unveil what lies beneath its veil, you would see the beloved as an old woman, and she is pleased only with the killing of her lovers. How often has she coquettishly tormented them with her disobedience, making them taste the chill of the month of Kanun of false hopes, and then they are in the midst of the heat of Tammuz. You seek a share with those who take booty, yet you did not witness the battle; the spoils are lawful only for those who were present at the encounter. Trials reveal the true worth of men, and how quickly the pretender is exposed!

*Your eyes sleep while you complain of passion;
had you truly been passionate, you would not be like this.*

O you who prefer what perishes over what endures, this is the opinion of your desire; why then do you not consult the intellect, so that you may learn which of the two is the better counsellor for you? Do not belittle a small sin, like the weak grass from which ropes are twisted that pull ships.

Has not the scheme been exhausted against the dam of Sheba? Life has stripped off a garment that is not held back, and every breath is a thread that is drawn out of it.

You are a hired worker and have work to do, so postpone the garments of rest until the work is finished.

How many ships have sunk in a sea of longing! They travelled without asking what the dawn had done, nor how the shooting stars had leaned. Their journey away from them is their demand that they attain what they sought.

The brave man wears his heart over his armour, and the coward wears his armour over his heart.

The greatest of calamities is the caravan's repeated journey to the land of the beloved, bidding farewell to the abandoned encampments.

*And glory which, if others claimed it,
would make them liable for the crime of thieves.*

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 4 (part 2 of 2):

They attained the heavens and lowered themselves, *
Yet when noble souls are brought low, they have ascended.

If your resolve were true, the abodes of laziness would hurl you into the wilderness of seeking.

The discerning critic fears that the counterfeit will enter upon him and mix with his wealth, and counterfeiting is its ruin. This friend holds his tongue and says: "This has brought me to the watering-places."

Umar adjures Hudhayfah: "Am I among them?" And the one who mixes things is on the carpet of security.

When the night grows dark, the battle breaks out between sleep and wakefulness. Longing and fear are then at the vanguard of the army of vigilance, while laziness and indolence are in the battalion of heedlessness. When the adversary makes a true charge, he routs the soldiers of slackness and sleep, and victory and spoils are gained. Dawn does not rise before the shares have been divided, and the sleepers have no news of it.

The night-worshippers (al-mutahajjidun, those who perform tahajjud, the voluntary night prayer) stood on the feet of diligence beneath the veil of darkness, weeping over a time lost in other than union. The mounts of wakefulness kept traversing the wilderness of darkness, and their eyes of hope saw nothing but the destination, while the driver of resolve was saying:

O company of the night, the journey is good, so seize the travel by night,
For whoever sleeps the whole night does not arrive.

Until the breeze of dawn blew, and the singer rose, seeking the darkness of night. When he resolved to depart, the people clung to its skirts, weeping over the separation from the Beloved. When dawn broke, their driver sang. At morning the people praise the night journey. O you who consider the states of these people as great, ascend the ladders and you will arrive.

Whoever combines knowledge of the Sunnah with following it, the wondrous meanings are attributed to him, and they proclaim before the assembled witnesses: "He was born of a legitimate marriage, not of fornication." And whoever combines innovation with desire, the babbling of every kind is attributed to him, and they proclaim before the assembled witnesses.

O intelligent one, do not be deceived. When the rose opens its eye and sees the thorns around it, let it be patient in their neighborhood for a while, for it alone is sought, accepted, and smelled.

When one who desires this world speaks, his words are such that whenever he digs into the well of his heart and goes deep in deduction, the dust of greed collapses upon him and buries him.

When you see the garment of this world shrink away from you, know that it is an act of kindness toward you. For the Bestower did not withhold it out of stinginess, lest it be torn, but out of gentleness toward the striver, lest he stumble.

Search for the lost heart before beginning, for presence of heart is the first station of the prayer. When you alight there, you move on to the desert of meaning. When you depart from it, you kneel at the door of intimate supplication, and that is the first hospitality offered by the guest of wakefulness.

The veil is lifted from the eye of the heart. How can one who has not yet gone out into the desert hope to enter Makkah?

If the sight of a created being, on the day it was displayed before them, absorbed the perception of the women who beheld him, so that they cut their hands and did not notice, then what of the state on the Day of Increase?

If you love worship, your heart will be present in its performance. It was said to Amir ibn Abd Qays: "Do you not become heedless in your prayer?" He said: "Something more beloved to me than the Qur'an, until I am occupied with it."

Muslim ibn Yasar would not turn his face during his prayer until a side of the mosque collapsed, and the people of the market were alarmed by it, yet he did not turn. When he entered his house, his family would fall silent, but when he stood to pray they would speak and laugh, knowing he was absorbed.

It was said to one of them: "Indeed we are beset by whisperings in our prayer."

He said: "With what? With Paradise, the dark-eyed maidens, or the Resurrection?"

They said: "No, rather with the world."

He said: "For spears to clash over me would be more beloved to me than that. You stand in your prayer with your body, having turned your face toward the qiblah, while you have turned your heart to another region. Woe to you! This prayer is not fit as a dowry for Paradise, so how could it be fit as a price for love?"

A mouse saw a camel and was pleased with it, so it pulled its halter and followed it. When it reached the door of its home, the camel stopped and cried out in the language of the state: "Either you take a dwelling worthy of your Beloved, or a beloved worthy of your dwelling. Likewise you: either you pray a prayer worthy of your Worshipped, or you take a worshipped one worthy of your prayer."

Attend to your heart. If you see desire has tilted one of the two loads, place in the other side the remembrance of Paradise and Hell, so that the load is balanced. If desire overcomes you, seek help from the Lord of the heart, and He will help you bear the load. If the answer is delayed, send the guide of brokenness after it, and you will find it with those whose hearts are broken, for gentleness with weakness is greater, so multiply it as much as you can.

When the hen does not tenderly care for its young, go out and earn.

When the ant was weak of sight, it was aided with a strong sense of smell, for it finds the scent of food from afar. When the mole was blind, it was inspired, at the time of need for sustenance, to open a fly's [wings] so that it falls into it, and it takes from it what it needs.

The birds sing all day long. It was said to the frog: "What is with you that you do not speak?" She said: "With the sound of the flute, my voice would be disgraced, but the night becomes me more."

Do not neglect the care [of the Beloved]. The sorcerers came to fight Him and fight His messengers. The covenant of peace was cut, the crowns of contentment were set down, and the drink of union was spilled. So they stretched out their hands to what they had squeezed from the wine of desire, and behold, it had turned into vinegar. They dripped upon it, and became intoxicated with the drink of love. When love made them stagger, they were crucified upon the trunks of palm trees. How wondrous are resolves that nothing can turn back! "I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides" (Q 7:124). They prostrated to Him one prostration, and they did not lift their heads until they saw their places in Paradise. Then ecstasy overcame them and longing took hold of them, and they said: "Decide what you will decide; you can only decide [concerning] this worldly life" (Q 20:72).

The east wind passes over the dweller of al-Ghada,
And my heart is split that its breezes blow.
Recently near to the Beloved, though every soul's desire
Is wherever its beloved has alighted.

The camels of their grandfather crossed the wilderness of the night and did not feel the touch of fatigue, for the road to the Beloved is never long.

Far is it from the lazy or the bored,
But for the longing lover, it is near.

O you who are present with us with the intention of recreation, you are not with us. Return to the nests of laziness, for war is stabbing and striking. And O you who are leaving, turn back, for we have crossed al-Udhaib, and soon our news will reach you after a little while. And O you who are holding a wedding at al-Khayf in Mina, tears will teach you how to throw the pebbles at the Jamarat.

The guest of love has no hospitality except souls. When you see a lover and do not know to whom he has been given, place your hand on his pulse and mention to him whomever you wish to treat him with, for the pulse quickens at his mention.

The believers, "when Allah is mentioned, their hearts tremble" (Q 8:2). The heat of fear is the summer of melting, and the coolness of hope is the winter of rest. And whoever is treated gently, all his time is the spring season.

A eye that delights you when it sees you, and its sister
Weeps from long estrangement and separation.
So preserve for the one the lasting of her joy,
And promise the one you made weep a meeting.

When you are granted wakefulness, guard it in a house of seclusion, for the hands of company are a ruin. Beware of the company of the idle, for disposition is a thief. Do not befriend a sinner, nor trust him, for whoever betrays his first benefactor will not be faithful to you.

O joy of repentance, cling to the remembrance of solitude, for the cat of desire is a hunter.

Beware of approaching the edge of the nest and leaving the house of seclusion until the intentions of the young birds are complete, or else you will become the sustenance of the hunter.

Delight in solitude is birdlime, the first thing that sticks to the wing of a bird, and mixing with people entails confusion, the least of which is the scattering of resolve and the weakening of determination.

The least harm in a wolf falling among sheep, if some of them are not struck, is that the sheep become frightened.

If you are not among those entitled to inheritance, then be among the company that, when the division takes place, "those of kinship" are present (Q 4:8). Woe to you! Do not belittle yourself, for the repentant one is a beloved, and the one who denies is sound.

Your acknowledgment of bankruptcy is the eye of richness. Lowering your head in regret is elevation.

Acknowledging error is the very substance of being correct. The merchandise of servitude was displayed in the marketplace of sale, so the angels offered their price, saying, "We glorify You with Your praise" (Q 2:30). Adam said: "I have only the coins of bankruptcy, their stamp is: 'Our Lord, we have wronged ourselves'" (Q 7:23). It was said: "This is what is spent from the treasury of the Special."

The groaning of sinners is more beloved to us than the chanting of those who glorify.

If Gog is the nature and Magog is desire, and they were in the land of hearts and corrupted it, then seek help from the King with strength; He will place between you and them a barrier (Q 18:95).

Gather for Him resolutions as strong as iron ingots, then reflect on what you have sent ahead, so that the bellows of regret may blow, and it will need no one to say to you, "Blow" (Q 18:96). Strengthen the building of resolve by abandoning habits and customs. When the structure is firm, pour upon it the drops of patience. Thus did the saints before you build; then the enemy came, but they could not overcome it, nor could they find a breach in it. The days of the season narrowed, so hasten with the camels, lest the standing at Arafat escape you.

Do not drive if you have no camel. Do not draw the bow if it has no string. How many a person has spent his soul showing off, so that the creatures would praise him, and his soul perished, and the praise turned into blame! Had he spent it for God, it would have remained as long as time endures. The work of the showy one, with its prayer, is all husks. The showy one fills his provision bag with sand that weighs him down on the road, and it does him no good.

The scent of showing off is a carrion, from which the nostrils of hearts recoil. When the silkworm began to weave, the spider came, resembling it, and said: "You have a weaving, and I have a weaving." The silkworm said: "But my weaving is the robes of kings, and your weaving is the web of flies." And at the touch of need, the difference becomes clear.

When tears are mingled upon cheeks,
It becomes clear who weeps genuinely from who feigns weeping.

The pine tree bears fruit in thirty years, while the gourd tree grows up in two weeks. So it says to the pine: "The road you crossed in thirty years, I crossed in two weeks." And it is said: "To me a tree, and to you a tree." The pine said to it: "Wait until the autumn winds blow. If it holds firm, then your pride is complete." Sufism and poverty were in the places of the hearts, then they came to the outward garments. It was a patched cloak, then it became a profession.

Change your attire, O showy one, for it will make you say: "Take me!" The sword and the shield, to adorn your appearance, are a disgrace. The counterfeit's shame becomes evident at the test.

If you had seen the vanguard of the sincere at the front of the caravan, or heard the cry of lovers in the midst of the caravan, or witnessed the rearguard of those who seek forgiveness at the end of the caravan, you would have known that you have been cut off beneath the tree of Umm Ghaylan. Alas for the one who is cut off from the caravan, counting the stations!

Count the nights, one night after another,
Though I lived a lifetime without counting the nights.
And God may gather the two who were scattered,
Though each thought that they would never meet.

For what purpose is the going forth in desire and bankruptcy? And how long will the striving be in the company of Iblis? How many counterfeits in deeds, and how much deception!

Where shall I place you? Do you hear any rustle of them?

Do you know that their regret and grief have grown intense over preferring the base? By God, they would wish that they had divorced the world before consummation.

The eye of death closes, but not with lowered lids,
And the gaze of its seeker has been drowsy since he existed.
Ignorance took hold of him at his birth,
So the speech cried out, while the mind of the man was intoxicated.

Discipline benefits only the noble-born.

Were the colocynth watered with sugared water, it would come out only bitter.

The trees of athl, willow, poplar, and the like, even if water persisted in their roots, would never bear fruit. The cloud of desire has covered the wilderness of existence and rained upon the eastern and western regions of the earth, but the lowlands of your heart are lowlands that hold no water and grow no pasture.

Yet despite this, do not despair, for wine may turn into vinegar, but that happens only for the good of its origin.

Thought was cleared in the heart, in the house of recitation, so mention of the Beloved and His attributes arose, and longing rose on the foot of striving. O you who have not witnessed the beauty of Joseph, you do not know what afflicted the heart of Jacob.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 18:

﴿So patience is most fitting (fa-sabrun jamil)﴾, with no lamentation in it.

I said: I heard Shaykh al-Islam Ibn Taymiyyah, may Allah sanctify his soul and illuminate his tomb, say many times: "Allah mentioned the beautiful patience (al-sabr al-jamil), the beautiful forgiveness (al-safh al-jamil), and the beautiful avoidance (al-hajr al-jamil). So the beautiful patience is that with which there is no complaint, the beautiful avoidance is that with which there is no harm, and the beautiful forgiveness is that with which there is no reproach." End of quote.

Hassan ibn Abi Jabalah also said, regarding the words of the Most High ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾, "It is that in which there is no complaint." Ibn Abi al-Dunya also transmitted this as a marfu' report (traced to the Prophet ﷺ).

Mujahid said: ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾ means without lamentation (jaza').

Amr ibn Qays said: ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾ means contentment with the calamity and submission (taslim).

Some of the early scholars (al-salaf) said: ﴿So patience is most fitting﴾ means there is no complaint in it.

(A subtle point)

Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) said: There are three who have the greatest insight (firasa) among people: the ruler (al-Aziz) in the case of Yusuf, when he said to his wife: ﴿Honor his lodging; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.﴾

And the daughter of Shu'ayb, when she said to her father about Musa: ﴿Hire him; the best one to hire is the strong and trustworthy.﴾ And Abu Bakr about Umar (may Allah be pleased with both of them), when he appointed him as successor. In another narration: and the wife of Pharaoh, when she said: ﴿(He is) a delight of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him; perhaps he will benefit us, or we may adopt him as a son.﴾ [al-Qasas: 9].

Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may Allah be pleased with him) was the greatest of the Ummah in firasa, and after him Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him). The instances of his firasa are well known, for he never said of anything, "I think it is such-and-such," except that it was as he said.

Sufficient as evidence of his firasa is his agreement with his Lord in the well-known situations.

Sawad ibn Qarib passed by him, and he did not know him. Umar said: "My assumption has been mistaken, or this man is a soothsayer, or he knew soothsaying in the Jahiliyyah." When he sat before him, Umar said this to him. He said: "Subhan Allah, O Commander of the Faithful, you have not received any of your companions with the like of what you have received me with." Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) said to him: "What we were upon in the Jahiliyyah was greater than that. But inform me about what I asked you." He said: "You have spoken the truth, O Commander of the Faithful. I was a soothsayer in the Jahiliyyah." Then he mentioned the story.

Likewise Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him) was truthful in firasa. Anas ibn Malik (may Allah be pleased with him) said: I entered upon Uthman ibn Affan (may Allah be pleased with him), and I had seen a woman on the road and had contemplated her beauty. Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "One of you enters upon me while the trace of adultery is apparent in his eyes." I said: "Is it revelation after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)?" He said: "No, but it is insight, proof, and truthful firasa."

The firasa of the Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) is the most truthful firasa.

The origin of this type of firasa is from the life and light which Allah Most High bestows upon whomever He wills of His servants, so the heart comes alive through it and is illuminated, and thus its firasa hardly ever errs. Allah Most High said: ﴿Is one who was dead and We brought him to life and made for him a light by which he walks among the people like one whose example is in darkness, never to emerge from it?﴾ [al-An'am: 122]. He was dead through disbelief and ignorance, so Allah brought him to life through faith and knowledge, and made for him, through the Qur'an and faith, a light by which he is guided among the people upon the right path, and by which he walks in the darkness. And Allah knows best.

[Section: On the Love of Forms (ʿishq al-ṣuwar)]

We conclude the answer with a section concerning the love of forms (ʿishq al-ṣuwar), and the harms it entails, both immediate and deferred, even if they are multiples of what the one who mentioned them has mentioned. It corrupts the heart in itself, and when the heart is corrupted, the intentions, the words and the deeds are corrupted, and the breach of tawhid (thaghr al-tawhid) is corrupted, as has preceded and as we shall also establish, God willing, Exalted is He.

God, glory be to Him, related this disease only of two groups of people: the people of Lot (al-Lūṭiyya) and women. He informed of the love of the wife of the ʿAzīz for Yusuf, and what she sought from him and schemed against him with. He informed of the state to which Yusuf came through his patience, his chastity and his piety, although what he was tested with is a matter that none endures except one whom God has granted patience. For the act of committing a deed is in accordance with the strength of the motive and the removal of the impediment, and the motive here was at its utmost strength, and that is from several aspects:

The first: what God, glory be to Him, has set in the nature of man of inclination towards woman, as the thirsty inclines towards water and the hungry towards food. So much so that many people endure hunger and thirst but cannot endure abstaining from women. This is not blamed when it meets what is lawful; rather it is praised, as in the Kitab al-Zuhd of Imam Ahmad, from the hadith of Yusuf ibn ʿAṭiyya al-Ṣaffār, from Thabit al-Bunani, from Anas, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Women and perfume have been made beloved to me of your world, and I endure abstaining from food and drink but I cannot endure abstaining from them."

The second: Yusuf (peace be upon him) was a young man, and the desire of youth and its intensity is stronger.

The third: he was unmarried, having neither a wife nor a concubine to break the intensity of desire.

The fourth: he was in a land of estrangement, where the stranger can attain the fulfilment of his need there in ways that are not possible for him in his homeland and among his family and acquaintances.

The fifth: the woman was of high station and beauty, such that each of these two matters calls to committing the act with her.

The sixth: she was not refusing nor disdainful. For many people, the disdain and refusal of a woman removes their desire for her, because of the humiliation of submission and asking that they find in themselves. And many people are increased in desire and love by disdain and refusal, as the poet said:

"Love was increased in me by her refusal, / for the dearest thing to man is that which withholds."

People's natures differ. Among them is one whose love is multiplied when a woman gives and desires, and dwindles when she is disdainful and refuses. Some judge told me that his desire and appetite dwindle when his wife or concubine refuses and is disdainful, to the extent that he does not return to her. And among them is one whose love and desire are multiplied by denial, so his longing intensifies whenever he is denied, and he obtains a pleasure from achieving the opposite after its refusal and aversion, and the pleasure of attaining a matter after its difficulty, and the intensity of eagerness to attain it.

The seventh: she sought, desired and exerted effort, so she spared him the burden of seeking and the humiliation of desiring her. Rather, she was the desiring, humbled one, and he was the esteemed one, to whom desire is directed.

The eighth: he was in her house, under her authority and domination, such that he feared, if he did not obey her, harm from her. Thus the motive of desire and the motive of fear combined.

The ninth: he did not fear that she or anyone on her side would disclose him, for she was the seeking, desiring one, and she had locked the doors and hidden the watchers.

The tenth: he was outwardly her slave in the house, such that he entered, exited and was present with her and was not objected to. Familiarity preceded the seeking, and that is among the strongest motives. As it was said to a noble woman from among the nobles of the Arabs: "What drove you to fornication?" She said: "The nearness of the pillow and the length of the night," meaning the nearness of the man's pillow to my pillow, and the length of the night between us.

The eleventh: she sought help against him from masters of deceit and trickery; she showed him them and complained of her condition to them, so that she might be helped by them against him. And he sought help from God against them, and said: "And unless You turn away from me their scheming, I would incline towards them and be among the ignorant" [Yusuf: 33].

The twelfth: she threatened him with prison and humiliation, and this is a kind of coercion, for it is a threat from one who is likely to carry out what he threatened, so the motive of desire and the motive of safety from the hardship of prison and humiliation combined.

The thirteenth: the husband did not show any jealousy or manly pride that would separate them and keep each of them away from the other. Rather, the most he responded with was to say to Yusuf: "Turn away from this," and to the woman: "And ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed you were of the sinners" [Yusuf: 29]. Intense jealousy in a man is among the strongest barriers, and here no jealousy appeared from him.

Despite all these motives, he preferred the pleasure of God and fear of Him, and his love for God led him to choose prison over fornication: "He said: My Lord, the prison is dearer to me than what they invite me to" [Yusuf: 33].

He knew that he could not withstand turning this away from himself, and that if his Lord did not preserve him and turn away from him their scheming, he would incline towards them by his nature and be among the ignorant. This is from the perfection of his knowledge of his Lord and of himself.

In this story are lessons, benefits and wisdoms that exceed a thousand benefits, and perhaps, if God grants success, we shall devote them to an independent work.

[Section: On the Harms of Love (ʿishq)]

It is well known that there is no religious benefit nor worldly benefit in the love of forms; rather its religious and worldly harm is many times over what benefit may be estimated in it, and that is from several aspects:

The first: occupation with love and remembrance of the created being instead of love and remembrance of the Lord, Exalted is He. Thus the two do not gather in the heart without one overpowering the other, and dominion and victory belong to one of them.

The second: the torment of his heart by it. For whoever loves something other than God is tormented by it without doubt, as it was said:

"There is nothing on earth more wretched than a lover, though he finds love sweet in taste.
You see him weeping at every moment, fearing separation or longing.
He weeps if they are far, out of longing for them, and he weeps if they are near, out of fear of parting.
So his eye is hot at parting, and his eye is hot at meeting."

And love, though its possessor may take pleasure in it, is greater than the torment of the heart.

The third: his heart is a captive in the grip of another, who humiliates it, but in his intoxication he does not feel its affliction. So his heart is like a little sparrow in the hand of a child who makes it drink the basins of destruction, while the child plays and jests, as one of them said:

"You have possessed my heart with estrangement and harshness, while you, carefree, amuse yourself and play."

So the life of the lover is the life of a bound captive, and the life of the carefree is the life of the released, unshackled one.

"Free in the sight of the eye, yet he is a captive; sick, revolving upon the pole of destruction.
And a dead man who is seen in the form of a living one walking about, and for him there is no resurrection until the resurrection.
A man of overwhelming waves, in which his heart is lost; for him there is no presence until death."

The fourth: he occupies himself with it from the affairs of his religion and his world. There is nothing more wasteful of the interests of religion and the world than the love of forms. As for the interests of religion, they depend on gathering the scattered heart and its turning towards God, and the love of forms is the greatest thing that scatters and disperses it.

As for the interests of the world, they in reality follow the interests of religion; whoever loses his religious interests and they are lost to him, then his worldly interests are more and more lost.

The fifth: the calamities of this world and the Hereafter reach the lovers of forms more swiftly than fire reaches dry wood. The reason is that the heart, whenever it draws near to love and its connection to it strengthens, it moves further from God. The hearts most distant from God are the hearts of lovers of forms. When the heart is distant from God, calamities besiege it, and Satan takes charge of it from every direction, and when he gains dominion over it, he leaves no harm that he can inflict upon it except that he inflicts it. So what is the supposition about a heart in which its enemy has established himself, and the most eager of creation for its error and corruption, while its Friend has been distanced from it, and which has no happiness, joy or delight except in His nearness and His guardianship?

The sixth: when it becomes established in the heart, firmly rooted, and its authority strengthens, it corrupts the intellect, produces whisperings, and perhaps puts its possessor among the madmen whose minds are corrupted so that they do not benefit from them.

The reports of lovers concerning this are present in their places, and some of them are witnessed by sight. The noblest thing in man is his intellect, and by it he is distinguished from the rest of the animals. When he loses his intellect, he joins the dumb animal, and perhaps the state of the animal is better than his state. Did anything remove the intellect of the madman of Layla and his like except this? And perhaps his madness exceeds the madness of others, as it was said:

"They said: You have gone mad for the one you love. I said to them: Love is greater than what happens to madmen.
Love never lets its possessor recover all his days, whereas the madman is only struck down for a time."

The seventh: it may corrupt the senses or some of them, either corruption in meaning or corruption in form. As for corruption in meaning, it follows the corruption of the heart, for when the heart is corrupted, the eye, the ear and the tongue are corrupted; so he sees the ugly as beautiful, from himself and from his beloved, as in the Musnad, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ): "Your love for a thing makes you blind and deaf." It blinds the eye of the heart from seeing the faults and defects of the beloved, so the eye does not see them, and it deafens his ear from listening to justice concerning him, so the ear does not hear it. Desires veil defects, and the one who desires a thing does not see its faults, until when his desire for it departs, he sees its faults. So intense desire is a veil over the eye, preventing seeing the thing as it truly is, as it was said:

"I loved you when my eye had a veil over it; when it was cleared, I cut my breath blaming it."

One who is inside a thing does not see its faults, and one who has come out of it, who never entered it, does not see its faults either; one sees its faults only if he entered it and then came out of it. That is why the Companions who entered Islam after unbelief were better than those who were born in Islam. ʿUmar ibn al-Khaṭṭāb (may God be pleased with him) said: "The bonds of Islam will be undone strand by strand when there is born in Islam one who does not know the Jahiliyya."

As for the corruption of the senses outwardly, it weakens the body and exhausts it, and perhaps leads to its destruction, as is well known in the reports of those whom love has killed.

It was reported to Ibn ʿAbbas, while he was at ʿArafa, that a young man had wasted away until he became skin upon bone. He said: "What is his condition?" They said: "He has love (ʿishq)." Ibn ʿAbbas began seeking refuge with God from love throughout that day.

The eighth: love, as has preceded, is excess in affection, such that the beloved takes control over the lover's heart, so that it is never free of imagining him, remembering him and thinking of him, such that he never leaves his thought or mind. At that point the soul is occupied away from employing the animal and psychic power, so that power is idled, and by its idling there arise from afflictions upon the body and the spirit what is hard to cure and impossible to remedy, so his actions, attributes and purposes change, and all of that becomes disordered, so that people are unable to set it right, as it was said:

"Love at first is a stubbornness that brings with it and that fate drives.
Until when the youth plunges into the seas of passion, there come matters too great to bear."

The beginnings of love are easy and sweet, its middle is worry, preoccupation of heart and sickness, and its end is ruin and death, unless a care from God, Exalted is He, overtakes it, as it was said:

"Live free, for love at its start is hardship, at its middle is sickness, and at its end is killing."

Another said:

"He was infatuated with love until he loved, and when he took it up he could not bear it.
He saw a deep sea and thought it a wave, and when he came into it he drowned."

The fault is his, for he is the one who wronged himself, and he has sat beneath the well-known proverb: "Your two hands have tied it, and your mouth has blown on it."

(Section)

Allah the Exalted has mentioned of Yusuf the Truthful (al-Siddiq) the greatest degree of chastity (iffah). For the motive (da'i) that came together in his case had not come together in the case of anyone else. He was young, and youth is the vehicle of desire (shahwah). He was unmarried (azab), having nothing to compensate him. He was a stranger, away from his family and homeland, whereas a person who lives among his family and companions feels shame before them lest they learn of him and he fall from their eyes. When he is far from home, this barrier is removed. He was in the condition of a slave (mamluk), and a slave does not disdain what a free man would disdain. The woman was of high station and beauty, and the motive in her case was stronger than in one who lacks these qualities. She was the one who sought, so the burden of a man's approach and solicitation was removed, along with his fear of being refused. Added to the solicitation was complete desire and enticement (murawadah), which removes the suspicion of a test or trial, by which one would know his chastity from his immorality. She was in the seat of her authority and her house, in a place where she could know the moment of opportunity and the place that eyes cannot reach. In addition to that, she locked the doors so that she would be safe from a sudden intrusion by someone entering. She approached him with both desire and dread. Despite all this, he was chaste for the sake of Allah and did not obey her, and Allah and her master had a right over him in all of that. This is a matter which, had anyone else been tested with it, one would not know how his condition would have been.

If it is said: did he not intend (hamm) to do it?

It is answered that there are two responses:

The first is that he did not intend it at all; rather, "had he not seen the proof (burhan) of his Lord" is the view of some of them regarding the interpretation of the verse.

The second, which is the correct one, is that his intention was a passing thought (hamm khatarat), which he abandoned for the sake of Allah, so Allah rewarded him for it; and her intention was a persistent intention (hamm islar), for which she exerted her full effort, but she did not reach him. Thus the two intentions were not equal.

Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal (may Allah be pleased with him) said: intention is of two kinds: the intention of passing thoughts (khatarat) and the intention of persistence (islar). The intention of passing thoughts is not held against a person, while the intention of persistence is held against him.

[Section: The Cure for Passionate Love (ishq)]

The cure for this deadly disease is that he should know that what he has been afflicted with of this disease, which is opposed to monotheism (tawhid), comes only from his ignorance and the heedlessness of his heart toward Allah the Exalted. So he must first know the tawhid of his Lord and His sunnah, then perform the outward and inward acts of worship that occupy his heart and keep it from continuous preoccupation with it, and he should abundantly seek refuge and humbly supplicate to Allah, the Glorified, to turn this away from him, and he should return his heart to Him. There is no cure more beneficial than sincerity (ikhlas) to Allah, and it is the cure that Allah mentioned in His Book when He said: ﴿Thus, that We might turn away from him evil and immorality. Indeed, he was of Our sincere (mukhlasin) servants.﴾ [Yusuf: 24].

He, the Glorified, informed that He turned away from him the evil of passionate love and the immorality of the act through his sincerity. For when the heart is sincere and sincerely directs its deed to Allah, the love of forms cannot take hold of it, since it takes hold only of an empty heart, as the poet said:

Her love came to me before I knew love,
so it found an empty heart and settled there.

Let the intelligent person know that reason and the Law both require the attainment of benefits and their perfection, and the elimination of harms and their reduction. So when a matter presents itself to the intelligent person in which he sees both benefit and harm, two duties fall upon him: a cognitive duty and a practical duty. The cognitive duty is to know which of the two sides, benefit or harm, outweighs the other. When the preponderance becomes clear to him, it becomes obligatory for him to prefer what is more beneficial for him.

[Judging by Circumstantial Evidence]

To proceed: You asked about a judge or governor who rules by insight (firasa) and by the circumstantial indicators (qara'in) through which the truth becomes apparent to him, and who relies on signs (amarat) rather than only on the outward appearance of evidence (bayyinat) and confession (iqrar). He may even threaten one of the two litigants if it becomes clear that he is the wrongdoer, may strike him, and may question him about matters that reveal the true state of affairs.

Is that correct or mistaken? This is a major issue of great benefit and high standing. If the judge or governor neglects it, he loses many rights and upholds much falsehood. If he goes to excess in it and makes it his sole basis, disregarding the legal procedures (al-awda' al-shar'iyyah), he falls into various kinds of injustice and corruption.

Abu al-Wafa Ibn Aqil was asked about this question and said: "That is not judging by insight; rather it is judging by signs." If you consider the Shari'ah, you will find that it permits relying on this. Malik, may Allah have mercy on him, held that one may reach a determination through confession in accordance with what the judge sees. This rests on the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿If his shirt is torn from the front, then she has told the truth and he is one of the liars﴾ [Yusuf: 26]. For this reason we have ruled by the construction of a vault (azaj), by the abundance of wooden beams in a wall, by the knots of the bindings in a reed enclosure (khușș), and by what distinguishes the woman from the man in disputes.

Regarding the case of the perfumer and the tanner when they dispute over a hide, the carpenter and the tailor when they dispute over a saw and an adze, the cook and the baker when they dispute over a pot, and similar cases: is this anything other than reliance on signs? Likewise is the ruling by qafa (tracing lineage by physical resemblance) and the consideration of the case of the hermaphrodite (khunha) and the signs indicating one of his two states, the examination of the signs of the direction of the qiblah, and the lawth (presumptive indication) in the qasama (the oath procedure in cases of homicide). End of quotation.

Thus, if the judge is not a faqih (jurist with a discerning mind) in the signs, the indications of the situation, the recognition of its evidence, and the circumstantial indicators both of state and of speech, just as he is a faqih in the particulars and universals of the rulings, he will lose many rights belonging to their owners. He will also rule by what people know to be false without any doubt, out of reliance on an apparent outward aspect without attending to its inner reality and the circumstances surrounding it.

Here there are two kinds of fiqh that the judge must have. One is fiqh in the universal rulings of events. The other is fiqh in the reality of the case itself and the conditions of people, by which he distinguishes the truthful from the liar and the one who is right from the one who is wrong. He then matches one with the other, giving the reality its ruling from what is obligatory, and he does not make what is obligatory contradict the reality.

Whoever has a sense for the Shari'ah, and knowledge of its perfections and of how it includes the ultimate interests of the servants in this life and the hereafter, and of how it comes with the ultimate justice that encompasses all creatures, and that there is no justice above its justice and no benefit above what it includes of benefits, will see clearly that just governance (al-siyasah al-'adilah) is a part of it and a branch of its branches. Whoever knows its purposes and its foundations, and whose understanding of them is sound, will have no need, alongside it, for the governance of anything else whatsoever.

Governance is of two kinds: unjust governance, which the Shari'ah forbids, and just governance, which extracts the right from the wicked transgressor. The latter is part of the Shari'ah. Whoever knows it knows it, and whoever is ignorant of it is ignorant of it.

Do not forget at this point the words of Sulayman, the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ), to the two women who both claimed the child. David (ﷺ) ruled it for the elder, so Sulayman said: "Bring me a knife, that I may cut it between you." The elder consented to this, but the younger said: "Do not do it, may Allah have mercy on you; it is her son." So he ruled it for the younger. What could be better than attending to this apparent indication? He inferred from the elder's acquiescence to the division that she intended to console herself by sharing the younger's loss of her child; and from the younger's compassion for the child and her refusal to consent to this, that she was its mother. The thing that drove her to refuse was the mercy and compassion that Allah the Exalted placed in the heart of a mother. This indication grew strong in his mind until he gave it precedence over the confession, for he ruled it for her even though the elder had said: "It is her son."

This is the truth, for when a confession is made for a reason the judge has become aware of, he never pays any attention to it.

(Section)

This statement contains several aspects of cunning.

The first: their saying ﴿The wife of al-Aziz is soliciting her young man﴾. They did not name her, but described her by a attribute that proclaims the ugliness of her act, namely that she is a married woman. The committing of indecency by a married woman is more heinous than by one who has no husband.

The second: her husband is the *ʿAzīz* of Egypt, its chief and its greatest. This makes the indecency more shameful.

The third: the one she solicits is a slave, not a free man. This adds further to the ugliness.

The fourth: he is her "young man" who lives in her house and under her protection, so his status is that of a member of the household. This differs from one who seeks such a thing from a distant stranger.

The fifth: she is the one who solicits and pursues.

The sixth: her passion for him has reached every extent, so that her love has penetrated to the *shaghaf* of her heart.

The seventh: implicit in this is that he is more chaste, more righteous and more faithful than she, since she is the one soliciting and pursuing, while he refrains out of chastity, nobility and modesty. This is the utmost censure of her.

The eighth: they used the verb of soliciting in the present tense, which indicates continuity and occurrence both now and in the future, and that this is her habit. They did not say "she solicited her young man." There is a difference between your saying "So-and-so hosted a guest" and "So-and-so honours guests, feeds people and bears the burdens of others," for the latter indicates that this is his nature and custom.

The ninth: their saying ﴿Indeed, we see her in manifest error﴾, meaning that we find her act extremely repugnant. They attributed the repugnance to themselves. It is the habit of women to support one another in their desires and hardly ever see such things as ugly, just as men support one another in that. Since they found her act repugnant, this is evidence that it is among the worst of matters, one that should not be supported, and it is not fitting to assist her in it.

The tenth: in this speech and blame they combined for her both excessive passion and excessive pursuit, so she was not moderate either in her love or in her pursuit.

As for the passion, it is their saying ﴿She has indeed been seized by love for him﴾, meaning his love reached the *shaghaf* of her heart.

As for the excessive pursuit, it is their saying "she solicits her young man." *Al-murāwada* means seeking repeatedly, time after time. Thus they ascribed to her intense passion and intense eagerness for indecency.

Their cutting of their hands was a wound, a laceration by the knives, out of the astonishment caused by what they saw. Thus her verbal cunning was met by this practical cunning, and this was the utmost of cunning among women.

Among this is the saying of the wife of the Aziz about Yusuf (peace be upon him), when she showed the women who were blaming her for her love of him: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me.﴾

She informed them about his inner beauty through his chastity, and she informed them of the beauty of his inner self, and showed them the beauty of his outward appearance.

(Benefit)

The wife of the Aziz said to the women, when she showed them him so that they would excuse her for loving him: ﴿That is the one about whom you blamed me.﴾ That is, this is the one for whom I was infatuated and whose love overwhelmed me, so who can blame me for loving him, when his appearance is so beautiful? Then she said: ﴿And I did seek to seduce him, but he refused.﴾

That is, this beauty protected him. His inner self is more beautiful than his outer self, for he was at the utmost of chastity, purity and distance from indecency. The lover, even if his beloved is absent, does not let his tongue speak except of his beloved's virtues and praise.

Related to this is the saying of the Exalted about the people of Paradise: ﴿And He gave them radiance and joy.﴾ So He made their outward appearance radiant and their inner selves joyful. Similar to this is His saying: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord.﴾ Indeed, nothing is more desirable to them, more comforting to their eyes, or more delightful to their inner selves than looking at Him. So He made their faces radiant with beauty and gladdened their hearts by looking at Him.

**Section: On the one who prefers the immediate punishment and pains over the pleasure of forbidden union**

This is a chapter into which only two kinds of men enter. The first is a man in whose heart faith in the Last Day has taken firm root, and in the reward and punishment that Allah has prepared there for whoever disobeys Him. He therefore chooses the lesser of two losses and the easier of two punishments. The second is a man whose intellect has overcome his desire, so he knows the corruptions that lie in illicit sexual relations and the benefits of turning away from them, and so he prefers the higher over the lower. Allah, the Glorified and Exalted, brought both of these qualities together for Yusuf the truthful, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him. He chose the worldly punishment of imprisonment over committing the forbidden act. The woman said: ﴿And if he does not do what I command him, he will certainly be imprisoned and be among the humiliated.﴾ He said: ﴿My Lord, prison is more beloved to me than what they invite me to. And unless You turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant.﴾ So he chose prison over the indecency. Then he disclaimed to Allah any power or strength of his own, and declared that this was by nothing but Allah's help, His enabling and His support, not by his own self. So he said: ﴿And unless You turn away from me their plot, I might incline toward them and be among the ignorant.﴾

Therefore a servant should not rely on himself, his patience, his condition, or his chastity. Whenever he relies on these, Allah's protection abandons him and forsaking (khudhlan) surrounds him. Allah the Exalted said to the noblest of creation, the most beloved of them to Him: ﴿And had We not made you firm, you would have almost inclined to them a little.﴾

For this reason, among his supplications (ﷺ) was: "O Turner of the hearts, keep my heart steadfast upon Your religion." His most frequent oath was "No, by the One who turns the hearts." And how could he not be, when Allah revealed to him: ﴿And know that Allah intervenes between a man and his heart.﴾

It is the established way of Allah in His creation that whoever prefers immediate pain over forbidden union, it will bring him, in this world, complete happiness. And if he perishes, then his is the great success. Allah, the Exalted, does not waste what His servant bears for His sake. In some of the divine reports, Allah, the Glorified, says: "Those who bear hardship for My sake, I see what they bear." Whoever gives up anything of himself for Allah, Allah either preserves it for him or compensates him with something greater than it. For this reason, when the martyrs gave up their souls for Allah, Allah made them alive with Him, provided for. In place of the bodies they gave up for Him, He gave them green birds' bodies, in which their spirits roam freely in Paradise wherever they wish, and take shelter in lamps hanging beneath the Throne. And when they left their dwellings for Him, He gave them good dwellings in the Gardens of Eden. That is the great success.

Wahb ibn Munabbih said: There was a worshipper among the Children of Israel who worshipped in a cell (saw'a). A man from the Children of Israel came to a prostitute, offered her money, and said: "Perhaps you could tempt him." So one rainy night she came to him and called out to him. He looked toward her, and she said: "Take me in to you." He turned away from her and devoted himself to his prayer. She said: "O servant of Allah, take me in to you! Do you not see the darkness and the rain?" She kept at him until he admitted her. She lay down near him and began to show him her beauty until his soul called him to her. He said: "No, by Allah, not until I see how you endure the fire." He went up to the lamp and placed one of his fingers in it until it burned. Then he returned to his prayer, and his soul called him to her again. He went back to the lamp and placed another finger in it until it burned. His soul kept calling him, and he kept returning to the lamp until all his fingers were burned while she was watching. Then she fell down and died.

Imam Ahmad said: Ibrahim ibn Khalid narrated to us, Umayya ibn Shibl narrated to us, from Abdullah ibn Wahb, who said: I do not know it except that he mentioned it from his father, that a worshipper among the Children of Israel was worshipping in his cell. Then a group of misguided people said: "Let us bring him down with something." They went to a prostitute and said to her: "Expose yourself to him." So she came to him on a dark, rainy night. He was standing in prayer, and his lamp was blazing. He did not turn to her. She said: "O servant of Allah, the darkness and the rain! Take me in to you!" She kept at him until he let her in. She lay down while he was standing in prayer. She kept turning and showing him the beauty of her form until his soul called him to her. He said: "No, by Allah, not until I see how you endure the fire." He approached the lamp and placed one of his fingers in it until it burned. He said: Then he returned to his place of prayer. He said: His soul called him again, so he went back to the lamp and placed his finger in it again, until all his fingers were burned while she was looking at him. Then she fell down and died. When they woke in the morning, they went to see what she had done, and found her dead. They said: "O enemy of Allah, O hypocrite! You had intercourse with her and then killed her!" He said: They took him to their king and testified against him. The king ordered him killed. He said: "Let me pray two rak'ahs." He prayed, then supplicated: "My Lord, I know that You would not hold me accountable for what I did not do. But I ask You not to let me become a disgrace to the people of the towns after me." He said: Then Allah returned her soul, and she said: "Look at his hand!" Then she died again.

Umar would check on him when he was absent. A woman from the people of Madina fell in love with him. She mentioned that to some of her women, who said: "I will devise a way to bring him in to you." So she sat in wait for him on the road. When he passed by her, she said to him: "I am an old woman, and I have a sheep I cannot milk. If you would come in and milk it for me..." They were the most eager of people for good. He went in, but saw no sheep. She said: "Sit until I bring it to you." Then suddenly the woman appeared before him. When he saw that, he went to a niche (mihrab) in the house and sat in it. She sought him for herself, but he refused and said: "Fear Allah, O woman!" She did not desist from him, nor pay any attention to his words. When he refused her, she screamed at him. They came and she said: "This man came in to me, wanting me for himself." They pounced on him, beat him, and bound him. When Umar prayed the dawn prayer, he missed him. While he was in that state, they brought him in chains. They said: "A woman cried out for help at night, so we came and found this young man with her. We beat him and bound him." Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "Tell me the truth." So he told him the story exactly as it happened. Umar said to him: "Do you know the old woman?" He said: "Yes, if I see her I will recognize her." Umar sent for the women of her neighbors and old women, and brought them, and presented them to him, but he did not recognize her among them, until the old woman passed by him. He said: "This one, O Commander of the Faithful!" Umar raised his whip (durra) at her and said: "Tell me the truth!" So she told him the story just as the young man had told it. Abu al-Zinad said: A monk used to worship in his cell. He looked out from it and saw a woman, and became infatuated with her. He put his leg out of the cell to go down to her, but then the divine protection (ʿișma) came down upon him. A man said: "You came out of the cell to disobey Allah! By Allah, you will not return with me into my cell!" So he left it hanging outside the cell, and snow and rain fell upon it until it rotted and fell away. Allah thanked him for that deed and praised him in some of His books as "the one of the leg (dhu al-rijl)."

Mus'ab ibn Uthman said: Sulayman ibn Yasar was one of the most handsome of people. A woman entered his house, and her soul tempted him, but he refused her. She said: "Then I will expose you!" So he fled from his home, leaving her in it.

Jabir ibn Nuh said: I was in Madina, sitting with a man on some business. An elderly man of pleasant face and fine clothes passed by us. That man stood up to him, greeted him, and said: "O Abu Muhammad, I ask Allah to magnify your reward and to strengthen your heart with patience." The elderly man said:

*"My right hand in battle and my helper,
Yet my right hand has betrayed its own arm.
And I have become bewildered and dazed from bereavement,
A man burdened, whose bonds have grown tight upon me."*

The man said to him: "Rejoice, for patience is the believer's support, and I truly hope that Allah will not deprive you of the reward for your calamity." I said to him: "Who is this elderly man?" He said: "A man from us, from the Ansar." I said: "What is his story?" He said: "He was afflicted with the loss of his son, who had been dutiful to him, who had provided for all his needs, and whose end was strange." I said: "And what was it?" He said: "A woman loved him and sent to him, complaining of her love and asking him to visit her. She had a husband, and she pressed him insistently. He confided this to a friend of his, who said: 'If you sent some of your family to her to admonish and rebuke her, I hope she would stop bothering you.' So he held back. She sent to him: 'Either you visit me, or I will visit you.' He refused. When she despaired of him, she went to a woman who practiced sorcery, and promised her great rewards to stir him up. The woman worked magic for her. Then one night, while he was with his father, the thought of her came to his heart, and a matter he had never known before was stirred in him, and his mind became confused. He got up quickly, prayed, sought refuge with Allah, while the matter grew more intense. He said: 'O father, catch me with a fetter!' His father said: 'My son, what is your story?' So he told him the story. His father got up, bound him, and put him into a room. He began to thrash and bellow as a bull bellows, then he grew calm, and he was dead, with blood flowing from his nostrils."
