This is not strange for men, but it is more remarkable in women. Abu Idris al-Awdi said: There were two worshippers among the Children of Israel, and there was a beautiful slave girl. Both of them fell in love with her, and each concealed his feelings from the other. Each hid behind a tree and looked at her. Each saw the other's secret, and they agreed to seduce her. When she came near them, they said to her: "You know our standing among the Children of Israel. If you do not yield to us, we will say in the morning that we found a man with you, and that he escaped from us, and that we seized you." She said: "I would never obey you in disobedience to Allah." So they seized her and said: "We found a man with her, but he escaped from us." Then a prophet of theirs came, and they set a chair for him. He sat on it and said: "I will judge between you." They said: "Yes, judge between us." He separated the two men and said to one of them: "Behind which tree did you see her?" He said: "Behind such-and-such tree." He said to the other: "And you?" He said: "Behind such-and-such tree," different from the one his companion had mentioned. Then fire came down from the sky and burned them both, and the woman escaped.

Abdullah ibn al-Mubarak said: Harun al-Rashid fell in love with one of his slave girls and wanted her. She said: "Your father has touched me." He became infatuated with her and said about her:

*"I see water, and I am severely thirsty,
But there is no way to reach it."*

*"Is it not enough for you that you own me,
And that people are to me like slaves?"*

*"And if you cut off my hand and my foot,
I would say out of contentment: You have done well, Zayd!"*

He asked Abu Yusuf about that, and he said: "Do we believe whatever a slave girl says?"

Ibn al-Mubarak said: I do not know which of the three I should marvel at more: Harun al-Rashid, for desiring her or for her desiring him; her, for turning away from him; or Abu Yusuf, for permitting him to approach her.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 40:

They worshipped only the names (al-musammayat), but they worshipped them because they had given them false names, such as al-Lat and al-'Uzza. These are merely false, untrue names that have no real referent (musamma) in actuality.

For they named them gods (ilah) and worshipped them, believing in the reality of divinity in them. Yet they possess no divinity beyond the mere names, not the reality of what is named. So they worshipped nothing but names that have no realities corresponding to what they designate. This is like one who names onion skins "meat" and eats them: it is said of him, "You ate nothing of the meat except its name, not its reality." It is also like one who names dust "bread" and eats it: it is said to him, "You ate nothing but the name of bread." Rather, this negation is even more forceful regarding their gods, for they have no reality of divinity in any respect. And there is no wisdom in them either, beyond a mere name.

So reflect upon this noble benefit in the words of Allah, the Exalted.

They said: God, glory be to Him, has struck similitudes and varied them in decree, in law, in wakefulness and in sleep. He directed His servants to take lesson (i'tibar) from this, to pass (ubur) from a thing to its like, and to reason from the like to the like. Indeed, this is the practice of the people of dream interpretation (ta'bir al-ru'ya), which is a part of the parts of prophethood and a kind of revelation, for it is built on analogy (qiyas), on comparison (tamthil), and on inferring the intelligible from the sensible. Do you not see that garments in interpretation are like shirts, and they indicate religion? Whatever in them is long or short, clean or soiled, is so in religion. Thus the Prophet ﷺ interpreted the shirt as religion and knowledge. The common element between them is that each covers its owner and beautifies him among people. The shirt covers the body, and knowledge and religion cover the spirit and the heart and beautify him among people.

[Dream visions and their interpretation] From this is the interpretation of milk as natural disposition (fitrah), because of what each of them contains of nourishment that brings about life and complete growth. A child, if left to his natural disposition, does not turn away from milk; he is naturally inclined to prefer it over anything else. Likewise is the disposition of Islam upon which God created mankind.

From this is the interpretation of cows as people of religion and goodness through whom the earth is cultivated, just as cows are so, along with their lack of harm, the abundance of their good, and the need of the earth and its people for them. For this reason, when "the Prophet ﷺ saw cows being slaughtered," that was a slaughter among his companions.

From this is the interpretation of seed and tillage as action, because the doer is a sower of good and evil, and what he has sown must come out for him, just as the crop of what the sower sowed comes out for him. The world is a field, deeds are the seed, and the Day of Resurrection is the day of the crop's emergence for the sower and its harvest.

From this is the interpretation of cut, propped-up timber as hypocrites, and the common element between them is that the hypocrite has no spirit, no shade, and no fruit; he is in the position of the timber that is likewise. For this reason God, may He be exalted, likened the hypocrites to propped-up timbers, because they are bodies empty of faith and good. In their being propped up there is another subtle point: when timber is put to use, it is placed in a roof, a wall, or other places of benefit. As long as it is left idle and unused, it is propped up, some of it against other parts. So He likened the hypocrites to timber in the state in which it is not put to use.

From this is the interpretation of fire as trial (fitnah), because each of them corrupts whatever passes over it and touches it. This one burns furniture, goods, and bodies, and that one burns hearts, religions, and faith.

From this is the interpretation of stars as scholars and nobles, because the guidance of the people of the earth comes about through each of them, and because nobles rise among people as stars rise.

From this is the interpretation of rain as mercy, knowledge, the Qur'an, wisdom, and the righteousness of people's condition.

From this is that the emergence of blood in interpretation indicates the emergence of wealth, and the common element is that the sustenance of the body depends on each of them.

From this is that impurity (hadath) in interpretation indicates impurity in religion. The minor impurity is a minor sin, and the major impurity is a major sin.

From this is that Judaism and Christianity in interpretation are innovation in religion. Judaism indicates corruption of intention and following what is other than the truth, and Christianity indicates corruption of knowledge, ignorance, and error.

From this is that iron in interpretation, and kinds of weapons, indicate strength and victory according to the essence and rank of that weapon.

From this is that a pleasant fragrance indicates good praise and goodness of speech and action, and a foul smell is the opposite. The scale indicates justice. The locust indicates armies, troops, and rabble who surge over one another. The bee indicates one who eats what is good and does righteous deeds. The rooster is a man of high resolve and far-reaching fame. The snake is an enemy or a person of innovation who destroys by his poison. Insects are the lowly of people. The mole is a blind man who begs people for alms. The wolf is a man who is oppressive, wrongful, treacherous, and wicked. The fox is a man who is treacherous, deceitful, cunning, and evasive of the truth. The dog is a weak enemy, much clamor and evil in his speech and abuse, or a man of innovation who follows his desire and prefers it over his religion. The tomcat is the slave or servant who goes around the household. The mouse is an evil, corrupt, sinful woman. The lion is a dominant, overpowering man. The ram is an unassailable man who is followed.

Among the general rules of interpretation: whatever is a vessel for water indicates furniture; whatever is a vessel for wealth, such as a chest, a bag, or a saddlebag, indicates the heart; whatever is penetrated, one part within another, mixed and blended, indicates partnership and cooperation or marriage; every fall and descent from high to low is blameworthy; every ascent and rise is praiseworthy when it does not exceed custom and befits the one who has it. Whatever fire has burned is a calamity, and its righteousness and its life are not hoped for. Likewise is what has broken of vessels that cannot be mended the way they were. 

Whatever is snatched or stolen in a way that its snatcher or thief is not seen is lost and not hoped for. Whatever its snatcher, thief, or place is known, or that has not disappeared from the eye of its owner, its return is hoped for. Every praiseworthy increase in the body, stature, tongue, penis, beard, hand, or foot is an increase of good. Every increase exceeding the limit in these is blameworthy, evil, and disgrace.

Whoever sees clothing in a place other than its specific place is reprehensible, such as a turban on the foot, a shoe on the head, or a necklace on the leg. Whoever is appointed as a judge, or made a deputy, or given command, or made a minister, or delivered a sermon, while he is not fit for that, will receive a calamity from the world, evil, disgrace, and an ugly reputation. Whatever clothing is disliked, its worn-out state is easier for its wearer than its new state. Walnuts are hoarded wealth; if it rots, it is ugly and evil. Whoever has feathers or a wing has wealth, and if he flies he travels. A sick person's going out of his house silently indicates his death, and speaking indicates his life. Going out through narrow doors indicates deliverance and safety from an evil and constriction in which one is, and repentance. This is especially so if the going out is into an open space and wide expanse, which is pure good. Travel and moving from place to place is a transition from one state to another, according to the condition of the two places.

Whoever in a dream returns to a state he was in while awake, there returns to him what he lost of good or evil. A man's death may indicate his repentance and his return to God, because death is a return to God, He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then they are returned to God, their true Master﴾ [al-An'am: 62]. The one in pawn is held captive by debt or by a right owed to God or to His servants. A sick person's farewell to his family, or their farewell to him, indicates his death.

In sum, what has preceded of the similitudes of the Qur'an are all principles and foundations for the science of interpretation (ilm al-ta'bir) for whoever reasons well from them. Likewise, whoever understands the Qur'an interprets dreams with it in the best interpretation. The correct principles of interpretation are only taken from the niche of the Qur'an. Like a king seen in a locality where he has no custom of entering, it is interpreted as the humiliation and corruption of its people. A rope is interpreted as covenant, truth, and support. Drowsiness may be interpreted as security. Herbs, onions, garlic, and lentils are interpreted for the one who takes them as having exchanged something lower for what is better than it, of wealth, sustenance, knowledge, a wife, or a home. Sickness is interpreted as hypocrisy, doubt, and the desire for showing off. A nursing infant is interpreted as an enemy, due to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8]. Marriage is interpreted as building. Light is interpreted as guidance, and darkness as misguidance.

The orchard indicates deeds, and its burning indicates their nullification, due to what has preceded in the similitudes of the Qur'an. From here, 'Umar ibn al-Khattab said to Habis ibn Sa'd al-Ta'i, when he had appointed him as judge: "O Commander of the Faithful, I saw the sun and the moon fighting each other, with the stars between them in two halves." 'Umar said: "With which of them were you?" He said: "With the moon against the sun." He said: "You were with the sign that is erased. Go, you will not work for me in any work, and you will only be killed in confusion over the matter." So he was killed on the day of Siffin. It was said to an interpreter: "I saw the sun and the moon enter my belly." He said: "You will die," and he argued with His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So when the sight is dazzled﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 7], ﴿and the moon is eclipsed﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 8], ﴿and the sun and the moon are joined﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 9], ﴿On that Day man will say: Where is the escape?﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 10].

A man said to Ibn Sirin: "I saw with me four loaves of bread, and then the sun rose." He said: "You will die within four days." Then he recited His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We made the sun for it a guide﴾ [al-Furqan: 45], ﴿Then We withdraw it to Us, a gentle withdrawal﴾ [al-Furqan: 46]. He took this interpretation to mean that he carried his sustenance for four days. Another said to him: "I saw my bag filled with termites." He said: "You are dead." Then he recited: ﴿So when We decreed death for him, nothing indicated his death to them except a creature of the earth﴾ [Saba': 14]. The palm tree indicates the Muslim man and the good word, and the colocynth indicates the opposite of that. The idol indicates the evil servant who does not benefit. The orchard indicates deeds, and its burning indicates their nullification, due to what has preceded in the similitudes of the Qur'an. Whoever sees that he unravels yarn or cloth for his slaves a second time, he breaks a covenant and reneges on it. Walking upright on a straight path indicates his steadfastness upon the straight path. Taking to the side paths indicates his deviation from it to what opposes it. If two roads are presented to him, one to the right and one to the left, and he takes one of them, he is one of its people. The exposure of a person's private parts to him is a sin he commits and by which he is disgraced. His fleeing and escaping from something is deliverance and victory. His drowning in water is a trial in his religion and his worldly life. His clinging to a rope between heaven and earth is his holding fast to the Book of God and His covenant, and his adherence to His rope. If it breaks with him, he has departed from protection, unless he is a ruler, in which case he may be killed or die.

Dreams are, then, similitudes struck by the angel whom God has appointed over dreams, so that the dreamer may infer from what was struck as a similitude to its like, and pass from it to its resemblance. For this reason the interpretation of dreams is called ta'bir, which is an intensive form derived from ubur (passing over), just as admonition is called i'tibar and 'ibrah (lesson) because the one admonished passes from the like to its like. Had it not been that the ruling on a thing is the ruling on its counterpart, and the ruling on the like is the ruling on its like, this interpretation and this taking of lesson would have been void and no path to them would have been found. God, glory be to Him, has informed that He struck similitudes for His servants in more than one place in His Book, commanded them to listen to His similitudes, called His servants to understand them, to reflect upon them, and to take lesson from them. This is the purpose of them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 53:

If it is said: how then did he say, at the time his innocence became manifest, ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾?

It is said: this has been said by a group of exegetes (mufassirun), but others, greater than them, disagreed and said that this is the speech of the wife of al-Aziz, not the speech of Yusuf (peace be upon him). The correct view is with them, for several reasons. The first: it is connected to the woman's speech, which is her saying: ﴿Now the truth has become evident. It was I who sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful. [He said], "That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plan of the betrayers." And I do not declare myself innocent﴾.

Whoever makes it part of his (Yusuf's) speech needs to supply a statement (idmar qawl) for which there is no indication in the wording at all, and a statement in such a context is not omitted, lest it cause confusion. At best, it could bear two meanings, and the first speech is certainly more appropriate for it.

The second: Yusuf (peace be upon him) was not present at the time of this utterance of hers, for he was in prison when she said: ﴿Now the truth has become evident﴾. The context is explicit on this, for when the king sent to him calling him, he said to the messenger: ﴿Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands.﴾ So the king sent for the women and summoned them and questioned them, and his wife was among them. They testified to his innocence and integrity in his absence, and they could not say anything but the truth. The women said: ﴿Allah forbid! We know of no evil in him.﴾ And the wife of al-Aziz said: I sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful.

If it is said: but his saying ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plan of the betrayers﴾ is better taken as the speech of Yusuf (peace be upon him)—

that is, my delay in attending with his messenger was so that the king would know that I did not betray him regarding his wife in his absence, and that Allah does not guide the plan of the betrayers. Then he said: ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent; indeed the soul is a commander to evil, except what my Lord has mercy upon. Indeed, my Lord is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ This is part of his complete knowledge of his Lord and of himself, for when he had shown his innocence and integrity from what he had been accused of, he informed about the state of his own soul, that he does not purify it or declare it innocent, for it commands to evil; but the mercy and bounty of his Lord is what protected him. So he returned the matter to Allah after having shown his innocence.

It is said: this, although a group has said it, the correct view is that it is part of the woman's speech, for the pronouns are all in one sequence, which indicates this, namely the women's saying ﴿We know of no evil in him﴾ and the wife of al-Aziz's saying ﴿I sought to seduce him, and indeed he is of the truthful﴾. These are five pronouns, both explicit and implicit. Then there is connected to them his saying ﴿That is so he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾. This is exactly the one mentioned first, so nothing separates the speech from its arrangement, and no statement for which there is no indication is supposed within it.

If it is said: then what is the meaning of her saying ﴿that he may know that I did not betray him in his absence﴾?

It is said: this is part of the apology. She combined the apology with the confession. So she said "that" — i.e., my saying this and my acknowledgment of his innocence — "that he may know that I did not betray him by lying against him in his absence, although I betrayed him to his face at the outset. Now he knows that I did not betray him in his absence." Then she excused herself by her saying ﴿And I do not declare myself innocent﴾, then she mentioned the reason that prevented her from declaring herself innocent, which is that the soul commands to evil. Reflect on how wondrous the end of this woman is: she acknowledged the truth, excused herself regarding her beloved, then excused herself, then mentioned the factor that drove her to what she did, then concluded that with hope in the forgiveness and mercy of Allah, and that if He does not have mercy on His servant, he is exposed to evil. So weigh this against the assumption that this statement is the speech of Yusuf (peace be upon him), both in wording and in meaning.

Reflect on the disparity between the two assumptions. It is not unlikely that the woman said this while upon the religion of polytheism, for the people used to affirm the Lord, glory be to Him, and His right, even though they associated others with Him. And do not forget her master's saying to her at the first stage: ﴿And ask forgiveness for your sin; indeed, you were of the sinners.﴾

(Section)

And in the Sahih from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said:

"Seven will be shaded by Allah in His shade on a day when there is no shade but His: a just ruler; a young man who grew up in the worship of Allah; a man whose heart is attached to the mosques; two men who loved each other for the sake of Allah, gathered upon that and separated upon that; a man who was called by a woman of rank and beauty and said, 'Indeed I fear Allah, Lord of the worlds'; a man who gave charity and concealed it until his left hand does not know what his right hand has spent; and a man who remembered Allah in seclusion and his eyes overflowed."

Consider the saying of the Prophet ﷺ, "I am the master of the descendants of Adam, and I say so without boasting." How he informed of the favour and bounty of God upon him! He also informed that this statement did not proceed from him out of pride in himself over those beneath him, but rather to display the blessing of God upon him, and to inform the Ummah of the rank of their imam and leader before God and the exaltedness of his station with Him, so that the Ummah might know the blessing of God upon him and upon them.

This resembles the saying of Yusuf al-Siddiq to the ruler: ﴿Set me over the storehouses of the land; indeed, I am a knowledgeable guardian﴾.

His statement about himself in this manner, since it contained a benefit that returns to the ruler, to the nation, and to himself, was good. For he did not intend by it boasting over them. The source of the words and the motive behind them make them good or blameworthy, while their outward form is one and the same.

[Section: The difference between ʿilm (knowledge) and maʿrifah (recognition/gnosis)]

The difference between ʿilm and maʿrifah is in wording and in meaning. As for wording: the verb ʿarafa (maʿrifah) takes one object. You say: "ʿarartu al-dār" (I knew the house) and "ʿaraftu Zayd" (I recognised Zayd). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And he recognised them, but they did not recognise him.﴾ [Yūsuf 12:58], and He says: ﴿They recognise him as they recognise their own sons.﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:146].

The verb ʿilm requires two objects, as in His saying: ﴿If you know them to be believing women...﴾ [al-Mumtaḥanah 60:10]. If it takes one object, it carries the meaning of maʿrifah, as in His saying: ﴿And others besides them whom you do not know; Allah knows them.﴾ [al-Anfāl 8:60]

As for the difference in meaning, it is in several respects:

The first: maʿrifah relates to the essence of a thing, while ʿilm relates to its states. You say: "ʿaraftu abāka" (I know your father), and "ʿalimtuhu ṣāliḥan ʿāliman" (I know him to be righteous and learned). For this reason, the command in the Qur'an is given with ʿilm rather than maʿrifah, as in His saying: ﴿So know that there is no god but Allah﴾ [Muḥammad 47:19], His saying: ﴿And know that Allah is severe in punishment﴾ [al-Mā'idah 5:98], and His saying: ﴿So know that it was revealed with the knowledge of Allah﴾ [Hūd 11:14].

So maʿrifah is the presence in the soul of the image of a thing and its cognitive likeness, whereas ʿilm is the presence of its states, attributes, and their attribution to it. Thus maʿrifah resembles conception (taṣawwur), and ʿilm resembles assent (taṣdīq).

The second: maʿrifah is, for the most part, of what was absent from the heart after having been perceived; so when one perceives it again, it is said: "ʿarafahu" (he recognised it). Or it concerns what has been described to one with attributes that have been established in one's mind; then when one sees it and knows that it is the one described by them, it is said: "ʿarafahu." Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And on the Day He gathers them, [it will be as if] they had not remained but an hour of the day, recognising one another among themselves﴾ [Yūnus 10:45]. He also says: ﴿And the brothers of Yūsuf came and entered upon him, and he recognised them, but they did not recognise him﴾ [Yūsuf 12:58], and He says: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognise him as they recognise their own sons﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:146], because his attributes were known to them; when they saw him, they recognised him by those attributes. And in the authentic hadith: "Allah the Exalted says to the last of the people of Paradise to enter it: 'Do you recognise the time in which you were?' He says: 'Yes.' He says: 'Wish,' and he wishes of his Lord." And Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And previously they used to seek victory over those who disbelieved, but when there came to them what they recognised, they disbelieved in it﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:89].

So maʿrifah resembles remembrance of a thing, which is the presence of what had been absent from remembrance. For this reason, the opposite of maʿrifah is denial (inkār), and the opposite of ʿilm is ignorance (jahl). Allah the Exalted says: ﴿They recognise the favour of Allah, then they deny it﴾ [al-Naḥl 16:83].

It is said: "ʿarafa al-ḥaqq fa-aqarra bihi" (he recognised the truth and acknowledged it), and "ʿarafahu fa-ankarahu" (he recognised it and denied it).

The third aspect of the difference: maʿrifah yields the distinguishing of the known from others, while ʿilm yields the distinguishing of what is described by it from others. This difference is other than the first, for the first returns to perceiving the essence and perceiving its attributes, whereas this one returns to separating the essence from other things and separating its attributes from the attributes of others.

The fourth difference: when you say "ʿalimtu Zayd" (I know Zayd), it conveys nothing to the listener, because he is still waiting for you to tell him in what state you know him. If you say "karīman aw shujāʿan" (generous or brave), the listener gains the benefit. But when you say "ʿaraftu Zayd" (I recognised Zayd), the listener learns that you have affirmed him and distinguished him from others, and he is no longer waiting for anything else. In reality, this difference is an elucidation of the difference before it.

The fifth difference, which is the difference of al-ʿAskarī in his Furūq and in the Furūq of others: maʿrifah is knowledge of the very thing in detail, distinguished from anything else, unlike ʿilm, which may relate to a thing in summary. This resembles the difference of the author of al-Manāzil, who said: "Maʿrifah is comprehension of the very thing as it is." On this definition, it is inconceivable that Allah could be known at all, and this category is wholly impossible regarding Him, for Allah the Exalted cannot be encompassed by knowledge, nor by recognition, nor by sight. He is greater than that, more majestic and mightier. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them, and they do not encompass Him in knowledge﴾ [Ṭā-Hā 20:110]. Indeed, the true meaning of this definition is the negation of the attachment of maʿrifah to the greatest of created things, even to the most manifest of them, which is the sun and the moon. Rather, it is not valid for anyone to recognise his own self and essence at all.

According to the people of this discipline (ahl hādhā al-sha'n), the difference between ʿilm and maʿrifah is that maʿrifah for them is the knowledge by which the knower acts in accordance with its requirement and its demands. They do not apply the term maʿrifah to the mere meaning of ʿilm alone; rather, they do not describe anyone as having maʿrifah except one who is knowledgeable about Allah, about the path leading to Allah, about its afflictions and its obstacles, and who has a state with Allah that bears witness to his maʿrifah. Thus the ʿārif (one who has gnosis) among them is one who knows Allah, the Exalted, through His names, attributes and actions; then he is truthful with Allah in his dealings; then he is sincere to Him in his intentions and aims; then he strips himself of his bad morals and afflictions; then he purifies himself from His filth, its stains and its transgressions; then he is patient with the rulings of Allah in His blessings and trials; then he calls to Him upon insight into His religion and His signs; then he dedicates the call to Him alone with what His Messenger brought, and does not mix it with the opinions of men, their tastes, their ecstasies, their analogies and their rational constructs, nor does he weigh against what the Messenger brought from Allah—upon him be the best of blessings—anything else. This is the one who truly deserves the name ʿārif, and when others are called by it, it is by claim and metaphor.

They have spoken about maʿrifah through its effects and signs. Some of them said: "Among the signs of maʿrifah of Allah is the arising of awe from Him; whoever's maʿrifah increases, his awe increases."

He also said: "Maʿrifah necessitates tranquillity; whoever's maʿrifah increases, his serenity increases."

One of our companions said to me: "What is the sign of the maʿrifah they point to?" I said to him: "The intimacy of the heart with Allah." He said to me: "Its sign is that one senses the nearness of his heart to Allah, and finds it near to Him."

Al-Shiblī said: "The ʿārif has no attachment; the lover has no complaint; the servant has no claim; the fearful one has no rest; and no one has any flight from Allah."

This is a fine statement, for true maʿrifah cuts from the heart all attachments and binds it to its object of knowledge, so no attachment to anything else remains in it. Attachments pass by it only as transients; they do not pass by in the manner of settling.

Aḥmad ibn ʿĀṣim said: "Whoever is more knowing of Allah is more fearful of Him." This is indicated by His saying: ﴿Only those of His servants who have knowledge fear Allah﴾ [Fāṭir 35:28], and by the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "I am the most knowing of you of Allah, and the most fearful of you of Him."

Another said: "Whoever knows Allah, the Exalted, the world becomes narrow for him with its vastness."

Another said: "Whoever knows Allah, the Exalted, every constriction becomes expansive for him."

There is no contradiction between these two statements. Every place that does not assist him in his affair and his objective becomes constricted for him, while what is constricted for others expands for him, because it is not in him, nor does he dwell in it with his heart, for his heart is not confined within it.

The first is at the beginning of maʿrifah; the second is at its end, the stage the servant reaches.

Another said: "Whoever knows Allah, the Exalted, his life is made pure; his living is good; everything reveres him; the fear of created beings departs from him; and he is intimate with Allah."

Another said: "Whoever knows Allah, his eye is comforted by Allah, his eye is comforted by death, and every eye is comforted by Him. Whoever does not know Allah, his heart is torn apart by sorrows over the world. Whoever knows Allah, no desire remains in him for anything other than Him. Whoever claims the maʿrifah of Allah while he desires something else, his desire has refuted his maʿrifah. Whoever knows Allah loves Him in proportion to his maʿrifah of Him, fears Him, hopes in Him, relies upon Him, turns to Him in repentance, is constant in His remembrance, longs for meeting Him, is shy before Him, and magnifies and exalts Him in proportion to his maʿrifah of Him. The sign of the ʿārif is that his heart is a mirror: when he looks into it, he sees the unseen to which he has been called to believe; according to the polish of that mirror, Allah, the Exalted, the Last Abode, Paradise and Hell, the angels, and the Messengers—may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon them—appear to him in it, as it has been said:

Ⅰ. When the pond is still with clarity, and kept from being stirred by the breeze,
Ⅱ. The sky appears in it without doubt, as do the sun and the stars.
Ⅲ. Likewise are the hearts of the possessors of manifestation, in whose clarity the Mighty Allah is seen.

This is the vision of the Highest Likeness (al-mathal al-aʿlā), as has been mentioned previously.

Among the signs of maʿrifah: that the Witness becomes manifest to you, the witnesses (other than Him) pass away, attachments are dissolved, obstacles are cut off, and you sit before the Lord, the Exalted, and stand and lie down in readiness to meet Him, as one who has tied up his baggage and resolved to travel sits in readiness for it, and stands and lies in that readiness, as a traveller alights at a station: he is standing, sitting, and lying down, in readiness.

It was said to al-Junayd: "Some people who claim maʿrifah say that they attain (virtue) by abandoning movements (of worship), as a matter of righteousness and piety?" Al-Junayd said: "This is the saying of people who speak of dropping the (religious) works, and it is grave in my view. The one who steals and fornicates is in a better state than the one who says this. Indeed, the knowers of Allah took their works from Allah and returned to Allah in them. Even if I remained a thousand years, I would not diminish from the works of righteousness the weight of an atom, unless I were prevented from them."

Among the signs of the ʿārif: he does not demand, does not dispute, does not reproach, sees no favour for himself upon anyone, and sees no right for himself upon anyone.

Among his signs: he does not grieve over what has passed, nor rejoice over what is coming, because he looks at things with the eye of passing away and perishing; for in reality they are like shadows and phantoms.

Al-Junayd said: "The ʿārif is not an ʿārif until he is like the earth, which the righteous and the wicked tread upon; like the cloud, which shades everything; and like the rain, which waters what it loves and what it does not love."

Yaḥyā ibn Muʿādh said: "The ʿārif leaves this world without having fulfilled his need of two things: weeping over himself, and praising his Lord." This is among the finest of statements, for it indicates his knowledge of himself, its faults and afflictions, and his knowledge of his Lord, His perfection and majesty. So he is severe in self-reproach and constant in praise of his Lord.

Abū Yazīd said: "They attained maʿrifah only by squandering what was theirs and standing with what belonged to Him."

He means: squandering their own portions (ḥuẓūẓ) and standing with the rights (ḥuqūq) of Allah, the Exalted and Most High, so that His rights suffice them in place of their portions.

Another said: "The ʿārif is not an ʿārif until, even if he were given the kingdom of Sulaymān, it would not occupy him from Allah for the blink of an eye." This requires explanation, for what is less than that occupies the heart; but his preoccupation with other than Allah is for the sake of Allah, and that is a preoccupation with Him, the Exalted, because when he is occupied with something else for His sake, he is not occupied away from Him.

Ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: "Maʿrifah rests on three pillars: awe, modesty, and intimacy." It was said to Dhū al-Nūn: "How did you come to know your Lord?" He said: "I knew my Lord through my Lord, and were it not for my Lord, I would not have known my Lord." It was said to ʿAbd Allāh ibn al-Mubārak: "By what do we know our Lord?" He said: "By His being above His heavens, upon His Throne, distinct from His creation." ʿAbd Allāh thus gave the root of maʿrifah, without which no one can have maʿrifah or affirmation of Allah, the Exalted, namely separation from creation and exaltation above the Throne.

Among the signs of the ʿārif: he withdraws from creation between himself and Allah, until it is as though they were dead, possessing no harm or benefit for Him, neither death nor life nor resurrection; and he withdraws his own self between himself and creation, until he is among them without a self. This is the meaning of the saying of one who said: "The ʿārif cuts the path in two steps: a step away from his self, and a step away from creation."

It was said: "The ʿārif is the son of his time," and this is among the finest and most concise of statements. He is occupied with the duty of his time, rather than with what has passed, which has become non-existent, and with what has not yet entered existence. His concern is the cultivation of his time, which is the substance of his enduring life.

Among its signs: he is at ease with his Lord, and he is wary of whoever cuts him off from Him. For this reason it was said: the gnostic (ʿārif) is one who is at ease with Allah, so that He makes him lonely with respect to creation; who is in need of Allah, so that He makes him independent of them; who is humbled before Allah, so that He honors him among them; who is humble before Allah, so that He raises him among them; and who is self-sufficient through Allah, so that He makes them in need of him.

It was also said: the gnostic is above what he says, and the scholar ('ālim) is below what he says. That is, the scholar's knowledge is broader than his state and his attributes, whereas the gnostic's state and attributes are above his speech and his reports.

Abu Sulayman al-Darani said: Allah Most High opens to the gnostic upon his bed what He does not open to him while he is standing in prayer. Another said: the gnostic's knowledge of God speaks upon his heart and his state while he is silent.

Dhu al-Nun said: everything has a punishment, and the punishment of the gnostic is his being cut off from the remembrance of Allah.

Some of them said: the show-off (riyāʾ) of the gnostics is better than the sincerity (ikhlāṣ) of the seekers (murīdīn). This statement, on its face, is extremely objectionable and needs explanation. The gnostic does not make a show before creation seeking standing in their hearts; rather, his showing is advice, guidance and teaching, so that he may be followed. He calls to Allah by his deeds just as he calls to Him by his words. He benefits from his knowledge and benefits others by it. The sincerity of the seeker is confined to himself. The gnostic combines sincerity with calling to Allah: his sincerity is in his heart, and he displays his deed and state so that he may be followed. The gnostic benefits by his silence, whereas the scholar benefits only by his speech.

"And if they were silent, the realities would praise you."

Dhu al-Nun said: the ascetics (zuhhād) are the kings of the Hereafter, and they are the poor among the gnostics. Al-Junayd was asked about the gnostic, and he said: "The color of water is the color of its vessel." This is a phrase by which he alluded to the reality of servanthood ('ubūdiyya): that he takes on the colors of the various kinds of servanthood. So while you see him praying, you then see him remembering, or reciting, or teaching, or learning, or striving, or performing pilgrimage, or assisting the guest, or aiding the distressed; and he takes a share in every spoil of these spoils. He is a worker with the workers, a learner with the learners, a fighter with the fighters, a prayer with the prayers, and a giver with the givers. He moves through the stations of servanthood from one servanthood to another, yet he remains devoted to one object of worship, and does not shift to any other.

Yahya ibn Muʿadh said: the gnostic is present yet distinct (kāʾin bāʾin). This may be explained in several ways.
Among them: he is present with creation outwardly, and distinct from them inwardly, in his secret and his heart.
Among them: he is present with his Lord and distinct from his self.
Among them: he is present with the people of the Hereafter and distinct from the people of this world.
Among them: he is present with Allah through agreement with Him, and distinct from people in their opposition to Him.
Among them: he is within things yet outside of them. For among people are those who are within things and cannot get out of them, and among them are those who are outside of them and cannot enter them; but the gnostic is within them and outside of them. This last is perhaps the best of these interpretations.

Dhu al-Nun said: the sign of the gnostic is threefold: the light of his knowledge does not extinguish the light of his scrupulousness (wara'); he does not hold an inner knowledge which the outer ruling (ḥukm) contradicts; and the abundance of Allah's blessings does not carry him to tear away the veils of Allah's prohibitions.

This is among the finest statements made about gnosis, and it needs explanation. For many people think that abstaining from things (tawaqquf) stems from little gnosis, whereas gnosis is broad in its breadth and wide in its expanses. The gnostic is expansive and made spacious, and expansiveness extinguishes the light of scrupulousness. So the gnostic's gnosis does not diminish his scrupulousness, nor does his scrupulousness contradict his gnosis. As one of them said: the gnostic does not reject any wrong, because of his insight into the secret of Allah in predestination (qadar). For him, witnessing predestination and the cosmic reality is the utmost of gnosis; and when he witnesses the reality, he excuses creation, because they are captives in the grip of predestination. Yet whoever excuses the people of major sins and transgressions, or even the people of disbelief, is the furthest of Allah's creation from scrupulousness; indeed, because of the darkness of his gnosis, he has extinguished the light of his faith.

His saying "the inner knowledge which the outer ruling contradicts" refers to what the deviants among those ascribed to the path (sulūk) hold. Experiences (adhwāq), ecstatic feelings (mawājīd) and inspirations (wāridāt) befall them which contradict the legal ruling, and these are known to them so that they cannot deny them. So they believe in them and leave the outer ruling for them. This is very widespread, and it is what the leaders of the Path criticized in these people; they cried out against them from every side and declared them innovators and misguided because of it.

His saying "nor does the abundance of Allah's blessings carry him to tear away the veils of Allah's prohibitions": the abundance of blessings makes the servant insolent, and carries him to spend them in their proper ways and in other than their proper ways. It calls him to use them for what is lawful and what is not lawful. Most of those who are blessed do not confine the spending of the blessing to the lawful measure, but exceed it to other things, and their souls make it seem to them that their knowledge of Allah will restore what the desires and transgressions have seized from them. They say: the gnostic is not harmed by sins as the ignorant is harmed. Sometimes it is made to seem to him that his sins are better than the acts of obedience of the ignorant. This is among the greatest of deceptions, and the matter is the opposite of that. The ignorant is tolerated in what the gnostic is not tolerated in; if the ignorant is punished double, the gnostic is punished double-double. The Law of Allah and His decree indicate this, and for this reason the punishment of the free person in the prescribed penalties (ḥudūd) is twice the punishment of the slave. And Allah Most High said concerning the wives of the Prophet ﷺ: ﴿O wives of the Prophet, whoever of you commits a clear indecency, the punishment will be doubled for her, twice over﴾ [al-Aḥzāb: 30]. So when a blessing is perfected upon the servant and he meets it with evil and disobedience, his punishment is greater; his rank is higher and his punishment is more severe.

He also said: he is not a gnostic who describes gnosis in the presence of the people of the Hereafter, so how much more in the presence of the people of this world? He means: it is not part of gnosis to describe gnosis to those who are not its people, whether they are worshippers or people of this world.

Abu Sa'id said: gnosis comes from the essence of existence (ʿayn al-wujūd) and from exerting effort (badhl al-majhūd). This is a fine statement, indicating that gnosis is the fruit of exerting effort in deeds and realizing ecstasy in states. It is the fruit of the work of the limbs, and the state of the heart is not attained merely by knowledge and inquiry. Whoever has no deed and no state has no gnosis.

Dhu al-Nun was asked about the gnostic, and he said: "He was here, then he left."

Al-Junayd was asked what he meant by this statement, and he said: a state does not confine him from another state, nor does a station veil him from moving through the stations. He is with the people of every station in the same way as they are, finding what they find, and he speaks of its landmarks so that they may benefit.

Muhammad ibn al-Fadl said: gnosis is the life of the heart with Allah.

Abu Sa'id was asked: does the gnostic reach a state in which weeping is withheld from him? He said: yes; weeping is only during the times of their journey to Allah. When they alight at the realities of nearness and taste the flavor of arrival from His kindness, that leaves them.

Some of the early predecessors (salaf) said: the sleep of the gnostic is wakefulness, his breaths are glorification, and the sleep of the gnostic is better than the prayer of the heedless.

The sleep of the gnostic is wakefulness because his heart is alive; his eyes sleep, but his spirit prostrates beneath the Throne before its Lord and Originator. His body is on the bed, and his heart is around the Throne. The sleep of the gnostic is better than the prayer of the heedless because the heedless one's body stands in prayer while his heart glorifies amid the trash of this world and its wishful thinking. For this reason his wakefulness is sleep, because his heart is dead.

It was said: sitting with the gnostic calls you from six things to six: from doubt to certainty, from show-off to sincerity, from heedlessness to remembrance, from desire for this world to desire for the Hereafter, from arrogance to humility, and from ill intention to sincere advice.

((The Eighth Part))

[Section]
My teacher, may God be pleased with him, said: Among things that may be thought to be of the same kind as the stratagems (ḥiyal) whose prohibition we have explained, but which are not of that kind, is the story of Joseph when God devised for him in taking his brother, as God recounts in His Book. For in it there are various kinds of good stratagems:

The first: his saying to his servants: ﴿Put their merchandise in their saddlebags, so that they may recognise it when they return to their family, so that they may come back﴾ [Yusuf: 62]. For he caused their return by this means. The scholars have mentioned several meanings for this:

Among them: that he feared they would not have silver with which to return; among them: that he feared taking the price from them would harm them; among them: that he wished not to take the price from them; among them: that he showed them his generosity in returning the merchandise, so that this would be more inviting to them to come back.

Among them: that he knew their trustworthiness would compel them to return to him to restore it. So this stratagem employed is a righteous act, and the aim was their return and the coming of his brother, and that is a matter with benefit for them, for their father, and for him. It is a righteous aim. He did not make himself known to them for other reasons, which also contain benefit for them, for him, and for their father, and the completion of what God willed for them of good in this trial.

The aim: their return and the coming of his brother, and that is a matter containing benefit for them, for their father, and for him, and it is a righteous aim. He did not make himself known to them for other reasons, containing benefit for them, for their father, and for him, and the completion of what God Most High willed for them of good in this trial.

Moreover, had he made himself known to them the first time, the gathering with them and with their father would not have taken that great place, nor reached that station. This is God's custom, glorified is He, regarding great and praiseworthy ends: when He wills to bring His servant to them, He prepares for them causes of tribulations, trials and hardships, so that his arrival at those ends after them is like the arrival of the people of Paradise to it after death, and the terrors of the barzakh, the resurrection, the gathering, the standing, the reckoning, the Bridge, and the bearing of those terrors and hardships. And just as the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was brought into Makkah by that great entry, after the unbelievers had expelled him into that predicament and granted him that mighty victory, after he had endured with the enemies of God what he endured.

The second kind: that when he equipped them with their provisions the second time, he placed the drinking-cup in his brother's saddlebag. This amount implied accusing his brother of being a thief. The scholars have said that this was by prior agreement with his brother and with his consent, and the right was his in this. This is indicated by the saying of God Most High: ﴿And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself, and said: Indeed I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾ [Yusuf: 69]. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: that he informed him that he was Joseph, and prepared him not to grieve over the stratagem he had employed to take him from them.

The second: that he did not explicitly tell him that he was Joseph, but meant: I am in place of your lost brother, so do not grieve over the harshness your brothers treat you with.

Whoever says this says: he placed the cup in his brother's saddlebag while the brother was unaware. But this contradicts what is understood from the Qur'an and what most scholars hold, and it involves frightening one who does not deserve to be frightened.

As for the first opinion, Ka'b and others said: when he said to him, "I am your brother," he said, "Then I will not leave you." Joseph said: "You know my father's grief over me; if I detain you, his sorrow will increase, and I cannot do this except after I expose you with a dreadful matter and attribute to you what cannot be borne." He said: "I do not care. Do whatever you wish, for I will not leave you." He said: "I will place my cup in your baggage, then call out against you for theft, so that I may have a means of retaining you." He said: "Do it." On this view, this action was done with the brother's permission and consent.

Similar to this kind is what the people of the biographies mention about 'Adi ibn Hatim: when his people intended apostasy after the Messenger of God (ﷺ), he restrained them from that and commanded them to wait. He used to order his son, when he herded the camels of charity, to go far away; when he came, he would argue with him before his people and intend to strike him, so they would stand and intercede with him for him. And he would order him every night to go further away. Then one night he ordered him to go very far, and he waited for him after night had fallen, while he blamed his people for their intercession and for preventing him from striking his son, and they made excuses for his son and did not deny his delay. Until, when the night had passed, he rode out in pursuit of him, overtook him, and drove the camels away until he brought them to Abu Bakr (may God be pleased with both of them). So the charities of Tayy were among what Abu Bakr was aided by in fighting the people of apostasy.

Likewise, in the authentic hadith, 'Adi said to 'Umar (may God be pleased with him): "Do you not know me, O Commander of the Faithful?" He said: "Yes, I know you: you embraced Islam when they disbelieved, you kept faith when they betrayed, you came forward when they turned away, and you recognised when they denied."

Similar to this is what the Prophet (ﷺ) permitted the delegation who wanted to kill Ka'b ibn al-Ashraf to say, and he permitted al-Hajjaj ibn 'Ilat in the year of Khaybar to say. All of this is permissible stratagem, because the owner of the right has permitted it and consented to it, and the matter employed in the stratagem is obedience to God and a permissible matter.

The third kind: a crier called out: ﴿O caravan, you are indeed thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70]. ﴿They turned towards them, saying: What is it that you are missing?﴾ [Yusuf: 71]. ﴿They said: We are missing the king's drinking-cup, and for whoever brings it is a camel's load, and I am its guarantor﴾ [Yusuf: 72] … to His saying: ﴿What is its penalty, if you are liars?﴾ [Yusuf: 74]. ﴿They said: Its penalty is that whoever is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty. Thus do We requite the wrongdoers﴾ [Yusuf: 75]. He began with their bags before the bag of his brother, then brought it out from his brother's bag. Thus did We devise for Joseph; he could not take his brother under the king's law, except that God willed﴾ [Yusuf: 75–76]. The scholars have mentioned two aspects regarding calling them thieves:

One of them: that it is of the kind of allusions (ma'arid), and that Joseph intended by it that they had stolen him from his father, since they had concealed him from him by the stratagem they devised against him and betrayed him in it; and a betrayer is called a thief. This is from speech of hidden meaning, and for this reason treasury embezzlers are called thieves (lusus). The second: that the crier was the one who said that without Joseph's command.

Qadi Abu Ya'la and others said: Joseph commanded some of his companions to place the cup in his brother's saddlebag, then one of the agents, when they had missed it and did not know who had taken it, said: ﴿O caravan, you are indeed thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70], on the suspicion that they were such, without Joseph's command to him. Or perhaps Joseph had said to the crier: "These have stolen," meaning that they had stolen him from his father, and the crier understood the theft of the cup, so he was truthful in Joseph's words and the crier was truthful. Consider the omission of the object in His saying: ﴿you are indeed thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70], so that it could be construed that their theft of Joseph was included, thus completing the allusion and making the speech truthful; and He mentioned the object in His saying: ﴿We are missing the king's drinking-cup﴾ [Yusuf: 72], and he was truthful in that. So he was truthful in both sentences together, by allusion and by explicit statement. Consider also Joseph's saying: ﴿God forbid that we take anyone except him with whom we found our property﴾ [Yusuf: 79], and he did not say "except whoever stole," which would be shorter in wording, out of striving for truthfulness, for the brother had not been a thief in any respect, and the property was rightfully with him. So the speech is among the finest and most truthful of allusions.

Similar to this is the saying of the two angels to David (peace be upon him): ﴿Two disputants, one of us has wronged the other﴾ [Sad: 22], to His saying: ﴿and he overcame me in argument﴾ [Sad: 23], i.e., he overcame me in speech. But to interpret this speech as allusion is hardly possible; rather its meaning is that it is speech that came in the form of a parable: i.e., if the matter is thus, how then is the judgment between us?

A parallel to this is the king's saying to the three whom God willed to test: "A poor man, a stranger, and a wayfarer, the ropes have been cut for me, and I have no means today except by God, then by you. So I ask you, by Him who gave you this wealth, for a camel by which I may reach my destination on this journey." This is not an allusion; it is explicit speech in the manner of a parable, and it gives the impression that I am the owner of this case, just as the two angels gave David the impression that they were the parties of the story, so that the trial might be completed.

For this reason Nasr ibn Hajib said: Ibn 'Uyaynah was asked about a man who apologises to his brother for something he has done, and distorts the account of it in order to please him: is he not sinful in that? He said: Have you not heard His saying: "He is not a liar who makes peace between people, saying what is good"? If he makes peace between himself and his Muslim brother, that is better than making peace between people, some of them with others; and that is when he intends by it the pleasure of God, dislikes harming the believer, regrets what he has done, and wards off its evil from himself, and does not intend by the lie to gain standing with them or to seek anything from them; for this has not been permitted, but it is permitted for him when he dislikes their displeasure and fears their enmity. Hudhayfah said: "I buy my religion with part of it for part, out of fear of committing what is greater than it."

Sufyan said: the two angels' saying, "Two disputants, one of us has wronged the other" [Sad: 22], intended the meaning of something, and they were not two disputants, so they did not thereby become liars. Abraham said: ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89], and said: ﴿Rather, this was done by their biggest one﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63], and Joseph said: ﴿You are indeed thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70]. Thus Sufyan made clear that these are permissible allusions.

(Section)
Among them: that when he equipped them the second time with their provisions, he placed the cup in his brother's saddlebag. This amount implies accusing his brother of theft.

It has been said that this was by agreement with his brother and with his consent, and the right was his, and he had permitted it, and his soul was content with it. This is indicated by the saying of God Most High: ﴿And when they entered upon Joseph, he took his brother to himself, saying: Indeed I am your brother, so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾ [Yusuf: 69].

This shows that he made his brother aware of who he was.

It has also been said that he did not explicitly tell him that he was Joseph, and that he only meant by his saying: ﴿Indeed I am your brother﴾ [Yusuf: 69]:

i.e., I am in place of your lost brother.

Whoever says this says: he placed the cup in his brother's saddlebag, and the brother was not aware of it. But the Qur'an indicates otherwise, and justice rejects it. Most of the people of tafsir hold a view contrary to it.

Among the subtle stratagems in this: when he wished to take his brother, he reached him by means that would make his brothers acknowledge it as right and just. Had he taken him by the authority of his power and rule, he would have been attributed to injustice and oppression, and he would have had no way under the king's religion to take him. So he reached taking him by a means that his brothers would recognise was not injustice, so he placed the cup in his brother's saddlebag by agreement with him. For this reason he said: ﴿so do not grieve over what they used to do﴾ [Yusuf: 69].

Among the subtle stratagems: he did not search their baggage while they were with him; rather he gave them time until he had equipped them with their provisions, and they had left the city, and then he sent in pursuit of them for this purpose.

Ibn Abi Hatim said in his tafsir: Ali ibn al-Husayn narrated to us, Muhammad ibn 'Isa narrated to us, Salamah narrated to us, from Ibn Ishaq, who said:
"He gave them time until, when they had set out and gone far from the town, he ordered them to be overtaken, then they sat down. Then a caller called out to them: O caravan, you are indeed thieves. They stopped, and his messenger reached them, and said to them, as they relate: Did we not honour your hospitality, and fill your measure, and treat you well, and do for you what we had not done for others, and admit you to us in our houses and dwellings? They said: Yes, and what of that? He said: ﴿You are indeed thieves﴾."

And it is mentioned from al-Suddi: "When they departed, a caller called: O caravan."

The context requires this, for if this had happened in his presence he would not have needed the call; a call is only a cry to a distant person, seeking his halting and detention.

So in this was a subtle stratagem: he removed the suspicion of complicity from the seeker by making it seem that he was unaware of what had been lost from him. It was as though, when the people departed and set out and separated from the city, the king needed his cup for some need, so he sought it, did not find it, asked those present, and they did not find it either, so they sent in pursuit of the people. This is better and further from detection of the stratagem than searching immediately before they had separated from him. Rather, the further they were from him, the more eloquent this meaning became.

Among the subtle stratagems: he proclaimed concerning them in a loud, high voice that all of them could hear, and did not address each one individually, announcing that the loss of the cup was a matter that had become known, with no concealment remaining, and that they had become famous for taking it, and no one else had been accused of it except them.

Among the subtle stratagems: the caller said "you are indeed thieves" without specifying what was stolen, until the people asked them about it. They said to them: "What are you missing?" They said: "We are missing the king's cup," so it became established among the people that the cup was the thing accused, and that they had lost nothing else. When this became apparent, they would not be wrong in accusing them with other than it, and their truthfulness and justice were shown in accusing them of it alone. This is among the subtle stratagems.

Among the subtle stratagems: the caller and his companions said to Joseph's brothers, peace be upon him: ﴿They said: What then is its penalty, if you are liars?﴾ — i.e., what is the penalty for one found to have stolen from you, and found with it? i.e., what is its penalty according to you and in your religion? ﴿They said: Its penalty is that whoever is found in his saddlebag, he himself is its penalty﴾ [Yusuf: 75].

So they seized them by what they had judged against themselves, not by the judgment of the king and his people.

Among the subtle stratagems: when the seeker intended to search their baggage, he began with their bags, searching them before the bag of the one with whom he was, to reassure them and to keep away the suspicion of collusion.

If he had begun with the bag of the one in whom it was found, they would have said: "How does he know it is in this bag and not in any of our other bags?" That would have been nothing but collusion and agreement. So he removed this accusation by beginning with their bags first. When he did not find it in them, he was about to turn back before searching the bag of the one in whom the drinking cup was, and he said: "I do not think you are thieves, nor do I think this one has taken anything either." They said: "No, by God, we will not leave you until you search his belongings, for that is better for your hearts and clearer for our innocence." When they insisted on this, they searched his belongings and brought out the drinking cup from them. This is one of the finest of stratagems. Hence the Exalted said: ﴿Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed it. We raise in degrees whom We will, and over every possessor of knowledge is one who knows.﴾ [Yusuf: 76]

Knowledge of an obligatory or recommended stratagem, by which one reaches the obedience of God and His Messenger, and by which the rightful is supported and the wrongdoer is defeated, is among the things by which God raises the servant's rank.

Regarding their being called thieves, the scholars have mentioned two explanations:

The first: it is of the category of allusions (al-ma'arid), and Joseph, peace be upon him, intended by it that they had stolen him from his father, since they had kept him away from his father through the trick they devised, and they had betrayed him in this matter. The betrayer is called a thief, and this is a well-known usage.

The second: the one who made the announcement said this on his own, without an order from Joseph, peace be upon him.

Qadi Abu Ya'la and others said: Joseph ordered one of his companions to place the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag. Then, when he missed it and did not know who had taken it, one of those charged with watching them said: "O caravan, you are surely thieves!", supposing that they were such, and Joseph, peace be upon him, had not ordered him to say that. Perhaps Joseph, peace be upon him, said to the announcer: "These have stolen," and he meant their theft of him from his father, while the announcer understood it as the theft of the drinking cup, and he spoke truthfully in his words: "Indeed you are thieves." He did not say: "the drinking cup of the king." Then, when he came to mention what was missing, he said: "We have lost the king's ..." and he was truthful in that. So the object was omitted in his words "thieves" and mentioned in his words "We have lost the drinking cup of the king." Likewise, Joseph, peace be upon him, said when they offered that one of them take the place of their brother: "God forbid that we take anyone except him in whose possession we found our property," and he did not say: "that we take anyone but a thief," for the property was indeed found with him, and he was not a thief. This is one of the finest allusions.

Sufyan ibn 'Uyayna was asked by Nasr ibn Hajib about a man who makes excuses to his brother for something he has done, and alters his words to please him: would he sin in that? He said: Have you not heard the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him:
"He is not a liar who makes peace between people and says what is good." (Or in the words that have come down: "He is not a liar who reconciles between people, and says good or conveys good.")

If he reconciles between himself and his Muslim brother, that is better than reconciling between people with one another, because he intends by it the pleasure of God and the avoidance of harming a believer. He regrets what he did, wards off its evil from himself, and does not intend by the lie to gain standing with them, nor to seek anything he might obtain from them. He was not given leeway in this, but was given leeway when he dislikes their displeasure and fears their enmity.

Hudhayfa ibn al-Yaman, may God be pleased with him, said: "I buy my religion with part of it, for fear of falling into something greater than it."

Sufyan said: The two angels said: ﴿Two disputants, one of us has wronged the other﴾ [Sad: 22]. He meant the sense of something, and they were not two disputants, so they did not thereby become liars.

Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said: ﴿I am sick﴾ [al-Saffat: 89] and ﴿Rather, this one, the biggest of them, did it﴾ [al-Anbiya: 63].

And Joseph, peace be upon him, said: ﴿You are surely thieves﴾ [Yusuf: 70], meaning, by it, their brother.

So Sufyan, may God have mercy on him, made clear that all of this is among the permissible allusions, even though it is called a lie, while in reality it is not a lie.

Some jurists have used the story of Joseph as evidence that a person may obtain his right from another by any means he can reach, without the consent of the one owing the right.

My shaykh said: This argument is weak. Joseph, peace be upon him, did not have the authority to detain his brother with him without his consent, and this brother had not wronged Joseph, so that it could be said he had taken retribution from him. Rather, it was the other brothers who had done that. Yes, his remaining behind from them was a source of harm to them, because of the harm to their father and because of the covenant he had taken from them, and in the covenant he made an exception with the words: ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66]. They were indeed encompassed, and Joseph, peace be upon him, did not intend by detaining his brother to take revenge on his brothers, for he was more noble than this. Although, within what he did, the harm to his father was greater than the harm to his brothers, that was a matter God commanded him, so that the decree might reach its term, and so that the trial by which Joseph and Jacob, peace be upon them both, deserved the perfect reward and elevated rank would be completed, and so that God's wisdom, which He had decreed and ordained, would reach its end. Even if it were supposed that Joseph, peace be upon him, intended retribution against them by what he did, this is not a point of disagreement among the scholars, for a man has the right to retaliate with the like of what was done to him. The point of disagreement is only whether he may betray the one who betrayed him, or steal from the one who stole from him. The story of Joseph, peace be upon him, was not of this kind.

Yes, if Joseph, peace be upon him, had taken his brother without his order, this argument would have some basis, though even on that supposition it would have no basis, for such a thing is not permitted in our law by consensus. And if Joseph had taken his brother and detained him without his consent, this would have been a trial from God for that one detained, like God's command to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son. In that case, what would have permitted it would be a specific revelation, like the revelation to Ibrahim, peace be upon him, to slaughter his son. And the wisdom in relation to the brother would be to test him and try him, so that he attains the rank of patience with God's decree and contentment with His judgment, and his situation in this would be like that of his father Jacob, peace be upon him, regarding Joseph's being kept away from him.

This is indicated by God's attributing that stratagem to Himself, with His words:
﴿Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed it.﴾ [Yusuf: 76]

He, glory be to Him, attributes to Himself the finest of these meanings, and whatever among them is wisdom, right and correctness, and recompense for the wrongdoer, and that is the utmost of justice and truth, as in His words: ﴿Indeed they plot a plot, and I plot a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 15-16], and His words ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted﴾ [Al 'Imran: 54], and His words ﴿God mocks them﴾ [al-Baqara: 15], and His words ﴿Indeed the hypocrites deceive God, and He is deceiving them﴾ [al-Nisa: 142], and His words ﴿And I give them respite; indeed My plan is firm﴾ [al-Qalam: 45].

This, from Him, glory be to Him, is in the highest degree of goodness, even if from the servant it is ugly and evil, because the servant is a wrongdoer in it, and it falls upon one who does not deserve it, whereas the Lord, exalted is He, is just in it, as it falls upon its people and those who deserve it. This holds whether it is said that it is a metaphor by verbal correspondence or by contrast, or that He named it so by correspondence with the name of what they did, or it is said that it is literal, and that the referent of these actions divides into blameworthy and praiseworthy, and the word is literal for both, as we have explained this meaning at length and fully discussed it in the book al-Sawa'iq al-Mursala 'ala al-Jahmiyya wa al-Mu'attila.

(Section)

Having understood that, Joseph, may God's blessings and peace be upon him, was the most skilled in stratagem in several respects.

The first: his brothers plotted against him, when they devised to separate him from his father, as Jacob, peace be upon him, said to him: ﴿Do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they devise a plot against you﴾ [Yusuf: 5].

The second: they plotted against him when they sold him as a slave, and said: "He is a runaway slave of ours."

The third: the plot of the Aziz's wife against him, by locking the doors and calling him to herself.

The fourth: her plot against him in her words: ﴿What is the recompense for one who intended evil to your wife, except that he be imprisoned or suffer a painful punishment?﴾ [Yusuf: 25].

She plotted against him first by seduction, and plotted against him second by lying about him, and therefore the witness said to her when Joseph's innocence became clear to him: ﴿Indeed it is of your guile; surely your guile is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28].

The fifth: her plot against him when she gathered the women for him and brought him out before them, seeking their help against him and making an excuse to them for her passion for him.

The sixth: the women's plot against him, until he sought refuge with God from their plotting, saying: ﴿And if You do not turn their plotting away from me, I shall incline toward them and become one of the ignorant.﴾ So his Lord answered him and turned away from him their plotting; indeed He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing [Yusuf: 33-34].

For this reason, when the messenger came with the order to leave prison, Joseph said to him: ﴿Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands. Indeed my Lord is Knowing of their plotting﴾ [Yusuf: 50].

If it is said: What was the scheming of the women who schemed against him, and which the Aziz's wife heard about, since God did not relate it in His book?

It is answered: Yes, He alluded to it with His words: ﴿And women in the city said: "The wife of the Aziz seeks to seduce her servant from himself; he has captivated her with love. Indeed we see her in manifest error."﴾ [Yusuf: 30].

This statement contains several aspects of scheming:

The first: their saying: ﴿The wife of the Aziz seeks to seduce her servant﴾ [Yusuf: 30].

They did not name her, but referred to her by a description that proclaims the ugliness of her act, by her being a married woman. The committing of indecency by her is worse than its committing by one who has no husband.

The second: that her husband is the Aziz of Egypt, its chief and its greatest, and that is worse for the indecency to occur from her.

The third: that the one she seeks is a slave, not free, and that is more grievous in ugliness.

The fourth: that he is her servant who is in her house and under her care, so his status is that of the household, unlike one who seeks this from a distant stranger.

The fifth: that she is the one who seduces and seeks.

The sixth: that her love for him has reached every extent, until her love for him has reached the core of her heart.

The seventh: that within this is that he was more chaste, more righteous and more faithful than she, since she was the one who seduced and sought, while he refrained, out of chastity, generosity and modesty, and this is the utmost censure of her.

The eighth: that they used the verb of seduction in the present tense, which indicates continuity and occurrence, both now and in the future, and that this is her habit. They did not say: "She seduced her servant." There is a difference between your saying: "So-and-so hosted a guest," and "So-and-so hosts guests, feeds food, and carries burdens." The latter indicates that this is his habit and custom.

The ninth: their saying: ﴿Indeed we see her in manifest error﴾ [Yusuf: 30].

That is, we find that extremely ugly in her, so they attributed the ugliness to her. It is the custom of women to support one another in desire, and they hardly consider it ugly, just as men support one another in that. Since they found that ugly in her, this was evidence that it is among the most ugly matters, and that it is not something she should be assisted in, nor is it good to help her with it.

The tenth: that in these words and this blame they combined excessive passion and excessive pursuit. So she was not moderate in her love, nor in her pursuit. As for passion, their words: ﴿He has captivated her with love﴾ [Yusuf: 30], that is, his love reached the core of her heart. As for excessive pursuit, their words: ﴿seeks to seduce her servant﴾ [Yusuf: 30]. And seduction (al-murawada) means pursuit time after time. So they attributed to her intense passion and intense eagerness for indecency. When she heard of this scheming from them, she devised for them a scheme more powerful than it: she prepared for them a couch, then sent for them, gathered them, and hid Joseph, peace be upon him, from them. It was said that she dressed him in the finest clothes she could, and brought him out before them suddenly, so that they were not prepared except that the most beautiful of God's creation had appeared before them unexpectedly. That dazzling sight overwhelmed them, and they had knives in their hands with which they were cutting what they ate, and they were so astonished that they cut their hands without realizing it. It has been said that they cut their own hands, but the apparent meaning is otherwise: their cutting of their hands was wounding them and slitting them with the knives, due to their astonishment at what they saw. Thus her verbal scheme was met with this physical scheme, and this was the utmost in scheming among women.

The purpose is this: God, glory be to Him, schemed for Joseph, peace be upon him, by bringing him together with his brother and taking him from the hands of his brothers against their will, just as they had taken Joseph from the hand of his father against his will. And He schemed for him by placing them before him in the position of the humbled, submissive, begging supplicants, so they said: ﴿O Aziz, adversity has touched us and our family, and we have come with meager merchandise, so give us full measure and be charitable to us. Indeed God rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

This humiliation and submission was in return for his humiliation and submission before them on the day they threw him into the well and sold him as a slave.

And He schemed for him by preparing for him the causes by which they, his father and his aunt, prostrated to him, in return for their scheming against him, out of caution about its occurring. For what moved them to throw him into the well was their fear that he would rise above them until they all prostrated to him, so they schemed against him out of fear of that. Then God, exalted is He, schemed for him until that came to pass, just as he had seen it in his dream.

This is like how Pharaoh oppressed the children of Israel: ﴿He slaughtered their sons and spared their women﴾ [al-Qasas: 4], out of fear that there would come forth among them one through whom his dominion would end. So God, glory be to Him, schemed against him, by bringing forth this child and raising him in his house, in his care, until what he feared came to pass through him, as it has been said:

*"If you fear a matter that has been decreed, and you flee from it, toward it you will be turned."*

(Section)

God's scheming, glory be to Him, falls into no more than two kinds.

The first: that He, glory be to Him, does an act outside the power of the servant against whom He schemes, so the scheme is pure decree, not of the domain of the Law, as He schemed against those who disbelieved, by taking vengeance on them with various kinds of punishment. Likewise was the story of Joseph, peace be upon him: the most Joseph could do was to put the drinking cup in his brother's saddlebag and send a crier to cry out: ﴿O caravan, you are surely thieves!﴾ [Yusuf: 70].
