When they denied it, he said: ﴿What is the penalty for it, if you are liars?﴾ They said: ﴿Its penalty is that he in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾ [Yusuf: 74-75].

That is, its penalty is that the owner of the stolen property enslaves the thief, either absolutely or for a term. This was the law of the family of Jacob, peace be upon him, to the point that it was said that such a thing was prescribed at the beginning of Islam: that when a debtor became insolvent, the creditor could enslave him, and the Prophet's sale of Surraq is to be understood in this way.

It has also been said that his sale was rather his hiring out to someone who would employ him, and his debt would be paid from his wages. On this view it is not abrogated, and it is one of the two narrations from Ahmad, may God have mercy on him: that a bankrupt person who still has debts and has a craft is compelled to hire out himself, or the judge hires him out and his debt is paid from his wages.

The saying of Joseph's brothers: ﴿He in whose saddlebag it is found, he himself is its penalty﴾ [Yusuf: 75] was an inspiration from God, a scheme against Joseph, peace be upon him, carried out through the tongues of his brothers, and that was outside his power. They could have escaped from it by saying: "There is no penalty upon him until it is proven that he is the one who stole, for the mere finding of it in his saddlebag does not make him a thief."

Joseph, peace be upon him, was just and would not take them without proof, and they could also have escaped by saying: "Its penalty is that you do to him what you do to thieves in your religion." Now, it was the religion of the king of Egypt, as is reported, that a thief is beaten and must pay back the value of what was stolen twice over. Had they said this to him, he could not have obliged them to something not required of anyone else. Therefore God, glory be to Him, said: ﴿Thus did We plan for Joseph. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless God willed it﴾ [Yusuf: 76].

That is, he could not have taken him under the law of the king of Egypt, because there was no way in his religion to take him.

His words ﴿unless God wills﴾ [Yusuf: 76] constitute a disjunctive exception: that is, but if God wills, He takes him by another means. It may also be connected, and the meaning would be: unless God prepares another cause by which he may be taken under the king's law, other than theft.

In this story there is an indication of acting upon a clear presumption in the hudud (prescribed punishments), even if no proof is established and no confession is made, for the presence of the stolen property with the thief is more truthful than testimony; it is a proof not subject to suspicion, and our law has taken this into account in several cases.

Among them: the presumption (lawth) in the qasama (oath procedure for homicide), and the sound view is that retaliation is carried out on that basis, as the authentic and explicit text indicates.

Among them: the Companions' (may Allah be pleased with them) punishment for wine-drinking based on its smell and vomiting.

Among them: the ruling of 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with him) concerning fornication established by pregnancy, which he made a counterpart to confession and testimony. So if the presence of the stolen item with the thief is not more manifest than all of this, it is not inferior to it.

When they searched his belongings and found the drinking cup (al-sawa') in them, that stood in place of evidence and confession. Therefore they could not complain of his seizure; and had this been an injustice, they would have said: "How does he take him without evidence or confession?"

We have fully discussed this matter in the book "al-I'lam bi-ittisa' turuq al-ahkam" (Informing about the Breadth of the Paths of the Rulings).

The point is that there is no doubt, let alone a proof, in the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) for the practitioners of legal stratagems (ahl al-hiyal).

For we have only spoken about the stratagems that a servant performs, and their ruling as to permissibility and prohibition, not about what Allah the Exalted plots for His servant. Rather, the story of Yusuf (peace be upon him) is an alert that whoever plots against another with a forbidden scheme, Allah the Exalted will certainly plot against him, and that He will certainly plot on behalf of the wronged one if he is patient under the plotting of his plotter and deals gently with it. So the believer who relies upon Allah, if the creation plots against him, then Allah the Exalted plots on his behalf and grants him victory, without any power or strength from him.

This is one of the two kinds of His plotting toward His servant.

The second kind: that He inspires him with a permissible, or recommended, or obligatory matter, which brings him to the good objective. Accordingly, His inspiring Yusuf (peace be upon him) to do what he did is also among His plotting, so He has plotted for him with both kinds of plotting. For this reason He, the Exalted, said: ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ [Yusuf: 76].

In this is an alert that precise knowledge of subtle stratagems that lead to the legislated objective which Allah and His Messenger love, such as supporting His religion, breaking His enemies, granting victory to the righteous and suppressing the falsifier, is a praiseworthy quality by which Allah the Exalted raises the servant's rank. Just as the knowledge by which one overcomes the falsifier and refutes his argument is a praiseworthy quality by which He raises the rank of His servant, as He, the Exalted, said in the story of Ibrahim (peace be upon him), his debate with his people, and his breaking of their argument: ﴿And that was Our argument which We gave Ibrahim against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ [al-An'am: 83].

Accordingly, there is a kind of plotting that is legislated, but it is not the plotting by which prohibited things are made lawful and obligatory things are dropped. For that is a plot against Allah and His religion, and Allah and His religion are the ones plotted against in this category. It is impossible for Allah to legislate this kind of plotting.

Also, this plotting is not complete except through an act whose intended purpose is other than its legislated purpose, and it is impossible for Allah the Exalted to legislate for a servant that he intend by his act what Allah has not legislated that act for.

Also, the legislated matter is general and not specific to one person over another. Whatever is permissible for one person is permissible for everyone whose situation is like his. So whoever resorts to a jurisprudential stratagem, whether forbidden or permissible, has no exclusive claim to that stratagem against one who does not understand or know it. Rather, the distinguishing mark of the jurist, when an incident occurs, is that he perceives its inclusion under the general ruling which he and others know. Allah the Exalted plotted for Yusuf (peace be upon him) only as a specific plot for him, as a reward for his patience and his excellence, and as a mention of it in the context of blessing upon him. These acts that Yusuf (peace be upon him) performed, and the acts that Allah the Exalted performed for him, if the discerning person reflects on them, he sees that they do not fall outside two categories:

The first: Allah's inspiring him to an act which was permissible for him to perform.

The second: an act performed by Allah upon him which is beyond the servant's capacity.

Both categories are distinct from the forbidden stratagems by which one seeks to drop obligations and make forbidden things permissible.

(Section)

Perhaps you say: you have greatly extended the discussion in this section, and it would have sufficed to allude to it.

It is said: rather, the matter is greater than what we have mentioned, and it is more deserving of elaboration. For the affliction and tribulation of Islam have been magnified by these two groups: the people of deceit and trickery, and of cunning in practical matters; and the people of distortion, sophistry and Qarmatian doctrines in matters of belief. Every corruption in religion, and indeed in worldly affairs, originates from these two groups.

By false interpretation 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him) was killed, the Ummah spread corruption in its own blood, some of it declared others disbelievers, and it split into seventy-odd sects. Thus what befell Islam through the interpretations of these people and the deception and cunning of those people befell it. Both groups gained control, their strength grew, and they punished whoever did not agree with them or rebuked them. But Allah refuses except to establish for His religion someone who defends it and clarifies its signs and realities, so that the proofs of Allah and His clear signs upon His servants do not become void.

[Section: An inference from the story of Yusuf and a comment upon it.]

Some jurists have argued from the story of Yusuf that it is permissible for a person to obtain his right from another by means which he is able to reach without the consent of the one who owes him the right.

Our shaykh (may Allah be pleased with him) said: This argument is weak. For Yusuf did not have the authority to detain his brother with him without his consent, and this brother was not one who had wronged Yusuf such that it could be said he had taken retribution from him. Rather, it was the rest of the brothers who had done that. Yes, his remaining behind with him would hurt them, because of their father's distress and the covenant he had taken from them. He had made an exception in the covenant by saying: ﴿unless you are encompassed﴾ [Yusuf: 66], and they were encompassed. Yusuf's purpose in detaining his brother was not vengeance against his brothers, for he was more noble than this, and in it there was harm to their father greater than the harm to his brothers. It was rather a command Allah commanded him so that the Book might reach its term, and the trial by which Ya'qub and Yusuf deserved the full reward might be completed, and Allah's wisdom which He had decreed for them might reach its end.

Even if Yusuf had intended retaliation against them by this, that is not the point of disagreement among the scholars. For a man may punish with the like of what was done to him. The point of disagreement is: may he steal or betray the one who stole from him or betrayed him, the like of what was taken from him or what was betrayed to him? The story of Yusuf is not of this kind. Yes, had Yusuf taken his brother without his command, this objector would have had a basis for doubt, though even then there would be no proof in it, for such a thing is not permissible in our law by consensus: that an innocent man be imprisoned and confined in order to take revenge upon another who has no crime. Had it been supposed that this happened from Yusuf, it must have been by revelation from Allah as a trial for that detained person, just as Allah tried Ibrahim with the slaughter of his son. The one permitting it in that case would be a special revelation, like the revelation which came to Ibrahim to slaughter his son, and its wisdom regarding the one tried would be his examination and testing, so that he might attain the station of patience with Allah's decree and contentment with His judgment. His condition in this would be like the condition of his father Ya'qub regarding Yusuf's being kept away from him. This is known from the jurisprudence of the story, its context, and the condition of Yusuf.

For this reason the Exalted said: ﴿Thus did We plot for Yusuf. He could not have taken his brother under the king's law, unless Allah willed. We raise in degrees whom We will, and above every possessor of knowledge is One All-Knowing﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. Thus Allah attributed this plotting to Himself, as He attributed it to Himself in His saying: ﴿Indeed they plot a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 15] ﴿and I plot a plot﴾ [al-Tariq: 16], and in His saying: ﴿And they plotted a plot, and We plotted a plot﴾ [al-Naml: 50], and in His saying: ﴿And they plot and Allah plots, and Allah is the best of plotters﴾ [al-Anfal: 30].

It has been said that calling that "plotting," "scheming," "mockery" and "deception" is by way of metaphor and the figure of reciprocity (majaz al-muqabalah), like: ﴿And the recompense of an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40], and like His saying: ﴿So whoever transgresses against you, transgress against him in the same manner as he transgressed against you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 194]. It has also been said, and this is more correct: rather, naming it so is literal and in its proper sense. For plotting is delivering a thing to another by a hidden way, and so are scheming and deception. But it has two kinds: the blameworthy, which is delivering that to one who does not deserve it, and the praiseworthy, which is delivering it to one who deserves it as a punishment for him. The first is blameworthy and the second is praiseworthy. The Lord, the Exalted, only does of that what is praiseworthy, as justice and wisdom from Him. He seizes the wrongdoer and the wicked from where they do not expect, unlike what the oppressors do to His servants.

As for "sayyi'ah" (evil), it is a form (fay'alah) from what is distressing (yasu'u), and there is no doubt that punishment distresses its recipient. So it is an evil for him, yet a good from the Wise and Just Judge. Knowing this: Yusuf the Truthful was plotted against more than once. The first was that his brothers plotted against him, scheming to separate him from his father. Then the wife of the 'Aziz plotted against him by displaying that he had solicited her, and then he was put in prison. Then the women plotted against him until he sought refuge in Allah from their plotting, and He turned it away from him. And Ya'qub said to him: ﴿Do not relate your vision to your brothers, lest they plot against you a plot﴾ [Yusuf: 5], and the witness said to the wife of the 'Aziz: ﴿Indeed it is of your plotting; indeed your plotting is great﴾ [Yusuf: 28], and he said: ﴿Return to your lord and ask him what is the matter with the women who cut their hands; indeed my Lord is Knowing of their plotting﴾ [Yusuf: 50]. So Allah plotted for him the best, subtlest and most just plot: He brought him together with his brother, and removed him from the hands of his brothers without their choice, just as they had removed Yusuf from his father's hand without his choice. He plotted for him in return for the woman's plot by bringing him out of the narrowness of prison into the expanse of kingship, and established him in the land to settle wherever he wished. He had in it the vindication of the women who had denied him and solicited him, until they testified to his innocence and chastity. He plotted for him in refuting the wife of the 'Aziz concerning herself, and her confession that she was the one who solicited him and that he was of the truthful. This is the outcome of one who is patient under the plotting of one who plots against him in wrongful transgression.

[Section: Allah's plotting is of two kinds.]

Allah's plotting does not fall outside two kinds. The first, which is the more prevalent, is that Allah the Exalted does an act beyond the capacity of the servant against whom He plots; so the plotting is a pure additional decree, not something of a forbidden category. Thus He plotted against the enemies of the messengers by punishing them with various kinds of punishments. Such was the story of Yusuf: the most that he could do was to place the drinking cup in his brother's baggage, and have a crier announce that they had stolen. When they denied it, he said: ﴿What is the recompense for it, if you are liars?﴾ [Yusuf: 74], meaning the recompense of the thief or the recompense of the theft. They said: ﴿Its recompense is: whoever is found in his baggage, he himself is its recompense﴾ [Yusuf: 75], meaning its recompense is the thief himself, whom the one robbed may enslave, either absolutely or for a period. This was the law of the family of Ya'qub.

[The construction of a sentence in the story of Yusuf]

Then, in the grammatical analysis of this statement there are two possibilities. The first: that His saying ﴿its recompense is whoever is found in his baggage﴾ [Yusuf: 75] is an independent sentence composed of a subject and predicate, and His saying ﴿he himself is its recompense﴾ [Yusuf: 75] is a second sentence likewise, emphasizing and confirming the first. The difference between the two sentences is that the first informs of the stolen one's entitlement to the thief's person, and the second informs that this is its recompense in our law and judgment. So the first is information about the one judged, and the second is information about the judgment, even though they are mutually implicative. And although the second conveys the sense of restriction, there is no recompense for it other than this. The second possibility: that the first ﴿its recompense﴾ [Yusuf: 74] is the subject, and its predicate is the conditional sentence, and the meaning is: the recompense of the thief is that whoever is found with the stolen item in his baggage is the recompense, just as you say: "The recompense of theft is whoever steals—his hand is cut off," and "The recompense of deeds is whoever does a good deed—ten times its worth, or an evil deed—one like it," and their like.

Our Shaykh, may Allah be pleased with him, said: The passage admits of the two meanings because "recompense" (al-jaza') may refer to the very ruling that the one who steals deserves punishment, may refer to the very act of punishing, and may refer to the very pain that reaches the one punished. The point is that Allah's inspiring them with this statement was a scheme (kayd) that He devised for Yusuf, one beyond their capacity. For they could have said: "There is no recompense upon him until it is established that he is the one who stole," since merely finding it in his baggage does not establish theft. Yusuf was just and would not seize them without proof. They could also have said: "Let him be treated as thieves are treated in your religion." In the religion of the king of Egypt, as the exegetes have said, the thief was beaten and made to pay twice the value of what was stolen. Had they said this, he could not have obligated them to what he did not obligate others to. For this reason Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf. He could not have taken his brother under the king's religion, unless Allah willed.﴾ That is, he could not have seized him under the religion of the king of Egypt, since there was no way in that religion for him to take him. On this basis, the words ﴿unless Allah willed﴾ are an exception of disconnection (istithna' munqati'), meaning: but if Allah willed, He took him by another means. Or it may be a connected exception in its proper sense, meaning: unless Allah willed that, and so He prepared for him a cause by which he could be held under the king's religion, from among the means by which a man was detained. When the scheme is understood as an act of Allah, namely that He eases for His believing servant who is wronged and relies upon Him matters by which his aim of taking vengeance upon the wrongdoer is achieved, this falls outside the legal stratagems (al-hiyal al-fiqhiyyah), for our discussion concerns the stratagems that the servant himself performs, not what Allah the Exalted does, as in the story of Yusuf.

A warning on the invalidity of stratagems, and that whoever devises a forbidden scheme, Allah schemes against him and deals with him in the opposite of his intention and in the manner of his deed. This is Allah's way with the practitioners of forbidden stratagems: He does not bless them in what they gain through these stratagems, and He prepares for them a scheme at the hand of whomever He wills of His creation, by which they are repaid in kind for their scheming and their stratagems.

[What the story of Yusuf indicates]
It also contains a warning that the believer who relies upon Allah, when people scheme against him, Allah schemes on his behalf and grants him victory without any power or strength of his own.

It also contains evidence that the presence of the stolen property in the hand of the thief is sufficient to establish the prescribed penalty (hadd) upon him. Indeed, it is equivalent to his confession, and it is stronger than evidence (bayyinah). The utmost that evidence yields is a conjecture (zann), whereas the presence of the stolen property in the thief's hand yields certainty (yaqin). On this basis the Sunnah came with the obligation of the prescribed penalty for pregnancy and for the smell of wine, as the Companions agreed. Using the story of Yusuf as proof for this is better and clearer than using it as proof for legal stratagems.

It also contains a warning that the hidden knowledge by which one reaches good aims is among the things through which Allah raises the servant's ranks. This is indicated by His words after it: ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾. Zayd ibn Aslam and others said: by knowledge. Allah the Exalted has informed of His raising the ranks of the people of knowledge in three places of His Book. The first is His words: ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Ibrahim against his people. We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ [al-An'am: 83]. He informed that He raises in degrees whom He wills through knowledge of the argument. He also said in the story of Yusuf: ﴿Thus did We devise for Yusuf... We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ [Yusuf: 76]. He informed that He raises in degrees whom He wills through hidden knowledge by which its possessor reaches praiseworthy aims. And He said: ﴿O you who believe, when you are told to make room in gatherings, make room, and Allah will make room for you; and when you are told to rise, rise. Allah will raise those of you who believe and those who have been given knowledge in degrees﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 11]. He thus informed that He raises the ranks of the people of knowledge and faith.

Section [The second type of Allah's scheme toward His servant]
The second type of His scheme toward His believing servant is that He inspires him to a matter that is permissible, recommended, or obligatory, by which He brings him to a good aim. Accordingly, His inspiring Yusuf to do what he did is also a scheme of Allah the Exalted. The words ﴿We raise in degrees whom We will﴾ [Yusuf: 76] point to this, for they contain an indication that subtle knowledge which leads to a legislated aim is a quality of praise, just as the knowledge by which one defeats the falsifier is a quality of praise. On this basis, some of the scheme is legislated, but it is not permissible to intend by it the scheme by which forbidden things are made lawful or obligatory things are dropped. For that is a scheme against Allah, and Allah is the One who schemes against the schemer. It is impossible that Allah the Exalted should legislate that His religion be schemed against. Moreover, that kind of scheme is not completed except by an act intended for other than its legislated purpose, and it is impossible that Allah should legislate for His servant that he intend by his act what Allah has not legislated that act for.

This is the answer to the argument of those who use stratagems by the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him. It has become clear that it is among the greatest proofs against them. And success is from Allah.

[Section: On guaranteeing what is not yet obligatory]

It is valid to guarantee what is not (yet) obligatory, such as saying: "Whatever I give to so-and-so is upon me," according to the majority of scholars, as the Qur'an indicates in the words of Joseph's caller: ﴿And for him who brings it, there is a camel-load [of grain], and I am its guarantor﴾ [Yusuf: 72].

Public interest requires this, and indeed need or necessity may call for it. According to al-Shafi'i (Shafi'i), it is not permissible; yet he accepted its permissibility when the cause of its obligation is clear, such as liability for the recovery of a sold item (darak al-mabi').

The legal device (hilah) for its permissibility according to this view is that if the guarantor agrees to take on a specific amount for him, it does not become obligatory upon him until the guaranteed party acknowledges it to the payer, and then the guarantor guarantees it on his behalf. If the acknowledging party fears that the creditor will demand it from him and he will not pay it to him, the device is that he says: "It is upon me from the price of a sale I have not received." If he is reluctant to report a falsehood, the device is that he sells to him what he wants to take from him at the sum that the guarantor has undertaken to pay; and when it becomes a debt on his responsibility, the guarantor guarantees it on his behalf.

This ruling applies when a man marries off his son, his slave, or his hired worker, and guarantees to the woman her maintenance and clothing. The sound view in all of these cases is the permissibility of the guarantee, and need calls for it, and there is no harm in it. It is not a contract of exchange (mu'awadah), so ambiguity does not affect it, and contracts of commitment (iltizam) are not affected by ambiguity, like a vow (nadhr). Then the ambiguity can be removed by setting a limit for him, saying: "From one dirham up to such-and-such."

If it is said: the amount between the dirham and the limit is unknown; he does not know how much is obligatory on him from it.

It is said: this does not undermine the validity of the commitment, because it will become clear later how much of it is actually obligatory. Moreover, if he acknowledges it and says: "He is owed by me what is between one dirham and a thousand," it is valid; likewise if he says: "I guaranteed on his behalf what is between one dirham and a thousand."

If it is said: the guarantor is a branch (far') of the guaranteed party (the principal); so when the principal has no obligation established in his responsibility, upon what does the guarantee rest and branch off? It is said: he becomes a guarantor only when the obligation is established in the responsibility of the one guaranteed; otherwise, at present, he is not a guarantor. And if it is correct to say, "he is a guarantor potentially," then in reality it is a guarantee conditioned upon a condition, and that is permissible. And God knows best.

[Section: Analogy of Resemblance (qiyās al-shabah)]

As for analogy by resemblance (qiyās al-shabah), God, glory be to Him, has related it only concerning those who falsely claim (al-mubṭilīn). Among its examples is the statement of God, exalted is He, reporting about the brothers of Joseph that when they found the drinking-cup in their brother's saddlebag they said: ﴿If he steals, a brother of his has stolen before﴾ [Yusuf: 77].

They did not join the original case (aṣl) and the derived case (farʿ) by a effective cause (ʿillah) or an indicator of it. Rather, they attached one of them to the other without any unifying indicator other than the mere resemblance that brought them together. They said: "This one is analogized to his brother; there is resemblance between them in many respects, and that one has stolen, so this one likewise." This is the joining by empty resemblance and the analogy by bare outward form, stripped of the cause that requires equality. It is a corrupt analogy. Sharing the kinship of brotherhood is not a cause for equality in theft, even if theft were a valid ground, and there is no evidence of equality in it. Thus the joining is based on a kind of resemblance empty of the cause and its indicator.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 84:

Hammam narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying, ﴿And his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing (his anguish)﴾, that he said: "He suppressed (his) grief and said nothing but good."

Yahya ibn al-Mukhtar narrated from al-Hasan: "al-Kazim (the one who suppresses) is the patient one (al-Sabur)."

Hammam narrated from Qatadah, regarding His saying, ﴿And his eyes turned white from grief, and he was suppressing (his anguish)﴾, that it means "kamid," that is, "kamad al-huzn," the sorrow of grief.

Al-Hasan said: "No two sips are more beloved to God than a sip of a painful, grief-causing calamity which its bearer repels with good consolation and patience, and a sip of rage which he repels with forbearance."

[Section: The Reality of al-Ghayba (absorption/rapture of the heart in its beloved)]

The author of al-Manazil (Sahib al-Manazil) said:

(Chapter on al-Ghayba) God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And he turned away from them and said, "Alas, my grief over Joseph!"﴾ [Yusuf: 84].

The way he derives evidence from the allusion of the verse is that when Ya'qub (ﷺ) was filled with love for Yusuf, peace be upon him, and with remembrance of him, he turned away from remembering his other son, despite the recency of his affliction by separation from him. He did not mention him in that state, nor did he grieve over him, being absent (mughayyab) from him through the love of Yusuf and his dominance over his heart. He also cited His saying, ﴿So when they saw him, they were struck with awe of him and cut their hands﴾ [Yusuf: 31], as evidence as well, for their witnessing of him in that state made them absent from the knives and from what they were cutting with, so that they cut their hands without perceiving it, and that is from the strength of al-ghayba.

(Fa'ida)

The ignorant person complains of Allah to the people, and this is the utmost ignorance of the one complained of and of the one to whom the complaint is made. For if he knew his Lord, he would not complain of Him, and if he knew the people, he would not complain to them.

One of the early pious predecessors (al-salaf) saw a man complaining to another man of his poverty and need, so he said: "O you, by Allah, you have done nothing but complain of One who is merciful to you."

And regarding this it has been said:

"When you complain to a son of Adam, you are only complaining of the Merciful to one who does not show mercy."

The gnostic (al-'arif) complains only to Allah alone, and the most knowing of the gnostics is the one who directs his complaint to Allah concerning himself, not to people. He complains of the things that necessitate people's dominance over him, looking to the words of the Exalted: ﴿And whatever affliction strikes you is because of what your hands have earned﴾, and His words ﴿And whatever good reaches you is from Allah, and whatever evil reaches you is from yourself﴾, and His words ﴿Why, when a misfortune strikes you, although you had inflicted twice as much, do you say: "From where is this?" Say: "It is from yourselves."﴾

So the levels are three: the lowest of them is that you complain of Allah to His creation; the highest is that you complain of yourself to Him; and the middle is that you complain of His creation to Him.

(Fasl)

Complaint is of two kinds. The first is complaint to Allah, and this does not contradict patience, as Ya'qub said: ﴿I only complain of my anguish and my grief to Allah﴾, alongside his words ﴿so patience is beautiful﴾. And Ayyub said: ﴿Harm has touched me﴾, while Allah described him as patient.

The master of the patient, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said: "O Allah, I complain to You of the weakness of my strength and the scarcity of my resources..." etc.

And Musa, may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him, said: "O Allah, to You is all praise, to You is the complaint, You are the One whose help is sought, through You is relief sought, upon You is reliance, and there is no power nor strength except through You."

The second kind is the complaint of the afflicted one by the tongue of state and speech. This does not combine with patience but opposes and nullifies it. The difference between his complaint and complaint to Him will be discussed later, in the chapter on the combination and separation of complaint and patience, God willing.

It has been said that patience is the bravery of the soul, and from here the saying was derived: "Bravery is patience for an hour." It has also been said that patience is the steadfastness of the heart at the points of turmoil. Patience and impatient wailing (al-jaza') are opposites, and for this reason one is contrasted with the other. The Exalted said about the people of the Fire: ﴿It is the same for us whether we wail or are patient; there is for us no escape﴾. Wailing is the companion and twin of weakness (al-'ajz), while patience is the companion of shrewdness (al-kays). If you asked Wailing "Who is your father?" it would say "Weakness"; if you asked Shrewdness "Who is your father?" it would say "Patience." The soul is the mount of the servant on which he travels to Paradise or the Fire, and patience for it is like the halter and the rein for the mount. If the mount has neither halter nor rein, it bolts in every direction.

And it has been memorized from the sermons of al-Hajjaj: "Restrain these souls, for they are eager for every evil. May Allah have mercy on a man who places for his soul a halter and a rein: he leads it by its halter to the obedience of Allah, and turns it by its rein away from the disobedience of Allah, for patience over the prohibitions of Allah is easier than patience under His punishment."

I say: The soul has two powers: the power of advance (iqdam) and the power of withdrawal (ihjam). The reality of patience is that one directs the power of advance toward what benefits him, and the power of withdrawal toward restraint from what harms him. Among people is one whose patience in doing what benefits him, and his steadfastness in it, is stronger than his patience in refraining from what harms him; so he endures the hardship of obedience but has no patience against the call of his desire to commit what He has forbidden. Among them is one whose patience in refraining from transgressions is stronger than his patience in the hardship of acts of obedience. Among them is one who has no patience for either this or that. The best of people are those most patient in both matters. Many people are patient in striving through night prayer in heat and cold, and in the hardship of fasting, yet have no patience to refrain from a forbidden glance.

Many people are patient in lowering their gaze and in not turning to images, yet have no patience for enjoining good and forbidding evil, and for striving against the disbelievers and hypocrites; rather, he is the weakest and most incapable of this. Most people have no patience for either of the two matters, and the fewest are those most patient in both situations.

It has been said: "Patience is the steadfastness of the motive of intellect and religion against the motive of desire and appetite."

The meaning of this is that nature demands what it loves, while the motive of intellect and religion prevents it, and the battle between them is ongoing, its outcome alternating, and the mover of this battle is the servant's heart, and patience, bravery and steadfastness.

**Ingenious benefit: the entry of (an) onto the verb**

The entry of *an* (أن) onto the verb, rather than settling for the verbal noun (*masdar*), has three benefits.

The first: the verbal noun may refer to the past or to the future without its form indicating which. So they used the derived verb, together with *an*, so that the statement about the event and the indication of time could be combined.

The second: *an* indicates that the act is possible, not necessary or impossible.

The third: it indicates the bare meaning of the event without the possibility of an additional meaning. Thus it protects the statement from ambiguity and clears it of the impurities of vagueness. The explanation: when you say "I disliked your going out" (*kurihtu khurujaka*) and "Your arrival pleased me" (*a'jabani qudumuka*), the sentence may carry several meanings. It may mean that the arrival itself pleased you, not some attribute or condition of it, although strictly speaking the arrival is not described by attributes but is a description of its modes. It may also mean that you were pleased by its speed or slowness, or by some state of it. But when you say "It pleased me that you came" (*a'jabani an qadimta*), the *an* before the verb serves as a clear marker that removes such vagueness from the mind. And similarly they added *an* after *lamma* in their saying: "*Lamma an jaa Zaydun akramtuka*" ("When Zayd came, I honoured you").

They did not add it after any temporal adverb except *lamma*.

This is because *lamma* is not in reality a temporal adverb (*zarf*) of time, but a particle indicating the connection of the second verb to the first, and that one of them is like the cause of the other. This differs from the temporal adverb: when you say "*Hina qama Zaydun qama 'Amrun*" ("When Zayd stood up, 'Amr stood up"), you have made one of them a time for the other by coincidence, not by connection.

Therefore they added *an* after *lamma* to preserve this meaning and to free it from the ambiguity that attaches to the adverb, since the temporal adverb is not a particle and so does not come for a meaning, as *lamma* does. The composition of *lamma* [is as follows].

Al-Farisi claimed that it is composed of *lam* and *ma*.

Al-Suhayli said: "I do not know what is meant by his statement that it is, in my view, among the particles whose form bears a resemblance to derivation and an allusion to a root from which it is taken, like what preceded regarding *sawfa* and *thumma*, because you say *lamamtu al-shay'* ("I gathered the thing") when you join parts of it together. This is a kind of that meaning toward which it is directed, because it links one act to another in the manner of causation or succession. When the causation is apparent, it is good to insert *an* after it as an indication of the meaning of the object of purpose (*maf'ul li-ajlihi*), even if it is not truly such an object, as in His saying: ﴿And when Our messengers came to Lot﴾ and ﴿And when the bearer of good news came﴾ and the like. When the succession is bare of causation, it is not good to add *an* after it. Consider this in the Noble Qur'an: [the difference between] the explanatory *an* (*an al-tafsiriyya*) and the verbal *an* (*an al-masdariyya)*."

As for the *an* that is explanatory, it is not, together with what follows it, in the sense of a verbal noun. Rather, it shares with the *an* mentioned earlier some of its meanings, because it secures what follows from possible interpretations and explains what precedes it of the vague verbal nouns that have the sense of statements and signs. It is therefore an explanation only of a verb that has the sense of the five modes of translation which reveal the speech of the soul. This is because the speech that subsists in the soul and is hidden from the senses, in the hearts, is revealed to the addressees by five means:

The utterance, the writing, the gesture, the counting on the fingers, and the setting of stones (*al-nasba*). These are the tongue of the state, and they are more truthful than the tongue of speech. So the explanatory *an* is only an explanation of what has been left vague among these means, as in your saying: "I wrote to him *an* go out," and "I gestured to him: go!"

﴿He was called out: Blessed is whoever is in the fire﴾

"I enjoined him *an* give thanks," "I tied a knot in my hand that I had taken fifty," and "I marked on my wall that they should not enter it."

From it is the saying of God, Mighty and Majestic: ﴿And He set up the balance, that you not transgress in the balance﴾

Here it is explanatory of the act of setting up, which is the tongue of the state.

Since the matter is so, it is the very same *an* mentioned earlier, because when it is explanatory it explains speech, and speech is a verbal noun. So it is, then, in the sense of a verbal noun. Only, you have placed after it a verb in the form of a command or prohibition, and that is an added benefit. An added benefit does not take the verb out of being a verb, and so it does not take it out of being verbal (*masdariyya*), just as the form of the past or the future after it does not take it out of that, when you say: "It pleases me that you stand" (*yu'jabuni an taqum*), and "that you stood" (*an qimta*).

So it seems that they intended the quiddity of the event while predicating it of the agent, not the event absolutely. For this reason, the *an* construction cannot be a subject whose predicate is a temporal adverb or a prepositional phrase, because the prepositional phrase does not attach to the meaning indicated by *an*, nor to that for which the verb was formed and derived from the verbal noun. Rather, the prepositional phrase attaches to the verbal noun itself, stripped of this meaning, as has been mentioned.

So it does not serve as a predicate of the preceding *an*, even though it is in the sense of a noun. Likewise, one does not predicate of it anything that is an attribute of the verbal noun, such as your saying: "A swift standing" or "a slow one," or the like. Such things are not predicated of the verbal noun.

If you say: "To stand is good" (*husna an taqum*) and "To act is ugly" (*qubha an taf'al*), this is permitted, because you mean by it the meaning of the object (*maf'ul*), as though you were saying: "I deem this good, or I deem it ugly."

Likewise, if you say: "*La-an taqum* is better than *an taq'ud*" ("To stand is better than to sit"), it is permitted, because it is a preference and a distinction. It is as though you were commanding him to do something, and you are not reporting on the event. The evidence is that this is impermissible in the past tense: you do not say "*In qamta* is better than *an qa'ada*," nor "*In qama Zaydun* is better than *an qa'ada*."

The impermissibility of this is evidence for what we have already set forth, that the event is what is reported on.

As for *an* and what follows it, although it is in the sense of a verbal noun, it has an additional meaning, and it is not permissible to report on it. Rather, it is intended and required, and it is commanded. If you find it as a subject with a predicate, the sentence is not to be taken in its outward sense, as has been explained regarding the construction of *lan*.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 100:

The saying of Yusuf to his father and his brothers: ﴿This is the interpretation of my vision from before. My Lord has made it true, and He was indeed kind to me when He brought me out of the prison﴾

He did not say, "He brought me out of the well," out of observance of etiquette (adab) towards his brothers, and out of consideration for them, so that he would not embarrass them with what had happened in the well.

He said, ﴿And He brought you from the desert﴾, and did not say, "He removed from you the hardship of hunger and need," out of etiquette towards them.

He attributed what had happened to its cause, and did not attribute it to the immediate agent, which was closer to him than the cause. So he said: ﴿after Satan had stirred up [discord] between me and my brothers﴾.

Thus he gave chivalry (futuwwah), generosity (karam) and etiquette (adab) their due. For this reason, the perfection of this character belongs only to the Messengers and Prophets, may God's blessings and peace be upon them.

From this is the command of the Prophet (ﷺ) to a man that he should cover his nakedness even when he is alone and no one sees him, out of etiquette towards God, in proportion to closeness to Him, glorifying and revering Him, having a deep sense of shame before Him, and recognizing His dignity.

Some of them said: "Keep to etiquette outwardly and inwardly. No one who wrongs etiquette outwardly is punished except outwardly, and no one who wrongs etiquette inwardly is punished except inwardly."

And 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, may God have mercy on him, said: "Whoever neglects etiquette is punished by being deprived of the Sunan (recommended practices). Whoever neglects the Sunan is punished by being deprived of the obligatory duties (fara'id). Whoever neglects the obligatory duties is punished by being deprived of knowledge (ma'rifah)."

It has been said: "Etiquette in action is a sign of its acceptance."

(Section)

The saying of Yusuf the Truthful: ﴿Indeed my Lord is Subtle in what He wills. Indeed, He is the All-Knowing, the All-Wise﴾

So he informed that He is gentle (latif) toward whatever He wills, bringing it about through hidden means that people do not know. His name al-Latif includes His knowledge of subtle things and His delivering mercy through hidden ways. From it comes tala††uf (gentle, discreet handling), as the People of the Cave said: ﴿And let him be gentle and let him not make anyone aware of you﴾. The apparent trials of Yusuf, namely his separation from his father, his being thrown into the prison, his sale as a slave, then the advances of the woman in whose house he was, who sought to seduce him and then lied against him, and his imprisonment, were afflictions and calamities; but their inner reality was blessings and opening, which God made a cause of his happiness in this world and the Hereafter.

This supplication gathers together the affirmation of Tawhid (the Oneness of God), submission (islam) to the Lord, the manifestation of need (iftiqar) before Him, disavowal of allegiance to anyone other than Him, the fact that dying upon Islam is the highest aim of the servant, and that this is in the hand of God and not in the hand of the servant, together with the acknowledgment of the Return (ma'ad) and the request to be in the company of the blessed (su'ada').

**(Section)**

If it is asked: what is the wisdom in the disbelievers being more numerous than the believers, and the people of the Fire being many times over the people of Paradise, as God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And most of mankind will not believe, however eager you are﴾; and He said: ﴿And few of My servants are grateful﴾; and He said: ﴿except those who believe and do righteous deeds, and few are they﴾; and He said: ﴿And if you obey most of those on earth, they will mislead you from the way of Allah﴾;

and (it is asked) about the sending forth of the Fire from every thousand, nine hundred and ninety-nine, and one to Paradise; and how this arises from a dominant mercy and an all-encompassing wisdom, and why the matter was not the opposite of that?

It is said: this question is among the clearest proofs for the view of the Companions (al-Sahaba) and the Successors (al-Tabi'un) on this issue, and that the matter returns to the mercy that encompasses all things and precedes wrath and overcomes it. On this basis, the question is dissolved entirely.

Then we say: the earthly substance necessitated the occurrence of variation within the human species, as in the al-Musnad and al-Tirmidhi, from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Indeed, Allah created Adam from a handful He took from all the earth, so among them are the good and the bad, the easy and the difficult, and other than that."

So the substance of the human species necessitated their variation in their characters, their wills, and their deeds. Then the wisdom of the Mighty, the Wise, required that the created being from this substance be tested with desire, anger, love, and hatred, and what follows from them. He tested him with his enemy, who does not fail to inflict harm and is never heedless of him. Then He tested him, along with that, with the adornment of this world and with the caprice (hawa) that he was commanded to oppose, despite its weakness and his need for it. It made the love of desires appealing to him: women, children, heaped-up piles of gold and silver, branded horses, cattle, and tilled land. He was commanded to leave off fulfilling his needs and desires in this present, immediate abode that is visible, for another abode whose ultimate goal is only attained therein after the world is folded up and passes away.

It was the requirement of human nature that none would remain steadfast under this trial, and that all of them would go along with the inclination of temperament and the impulses of anger and desire. But their Creator and Originator did not leave them to that. Rather, He sent His messengers to them, sent down His books upon them, clarified for them the places of His pleasure and His wrath, and promised them, in exchange for opposing their caprice and natures, the most perfect pleasures in the Abode of Bliss. Yet the minds of most people were not strong enough to prefer the deferred, awaited reward after the world's passing over this hastened, present, visible one. They said: "How can a present cash be sold for a delayed credit, a thing received by the hand for a promise that it will be attained after the world is folded up and the universe is ruined?" The tongue of the state of most of them says: "Take what you see and leave what you have only heard of."

So the divine success assisted whoever He knew to be fit for the places of His bounty. He strengthened him with a force of faith and an insight by whose light he saw the reality of the Hereafter and its permanence, and what Allah has prepared therein for the people of His obedience and the people of His disobedience. He saw the reality of this world, the swiftness of its ending, the scantiness of its fulfilment, the wrongdoing of its partners, and that it is, as Allah, glorified is He, described it: "play and diversion, boasting among its people, and rivalry in wealth and children," and like rain whose vegetation pleases the disbelievers, then it dries up and you see it turning yellow, then it becomes debris. We grew up in this abode, and we are of it, and its children; we know nothing else. Customs have ruled, the authority has subdued caprice, the call of the souls has supported it, the demands of temperament have urged it, and sense has overcome reason. Power belonged to it, and people follow the religion of the king.

There is no doubt that whoever tears through these veils, cuts these attachments, opposes customs, does not respond to the impulses of temperament, and disobeys the authority of caprice, will be only a few. For this reason, the fiery substance was less inclined toward this type than the earthly substance, due to the fire's lightness, its recklessness, its frequent movement, its swift motion, and its lack of stability. Water, the royal substance, was mixed with it, so the created being became entirely good. Thus the rational beings addressed are created from these three substances, and the wisdom required that they be upon this attribute and this constitution. Had they been otherwise, the purpose of testing and trial would not have been achieved, nor the variety of servitude, nor the manifestation of the effects of the Names and Attributes. Had the people of faith and goodness been the majority, the dominant ones, the benefit of striving (jihad) and its consequences, which are among the most excellent kinds of servitude, would have been lost, and the perfection that follows from it would have been missed. There is nothing better than what the wisdom of the Wisest of the wise required concerning the created being from these substances.

Then, glorified is He, He purifies what is in the created being of those two substances from defilement and evil, refines it, and extracts its goodness to the abode of the good, and casts its defilement where filth and impurities are cast. This is the ultimate of wisdom, as is the case with the precious substances of the ores that benefit people: gold, silver, iron, and copper. So the pure essence of these substances and their goodness is less than their dross and their impurity. People are the seed of the earth, and the pure good from the crop, after its chaff, its husk, its winnowing, and its straw, is less than the rest of its parts. Those parts are like the form for it, and the protection is like the firewood and thorns for the fruit, and the earth and stones for precious metals.

Commentary of Ibn al-Qayyim (al-Tafsir al-Qayyim) on surah 12, verse 108:

Al-Farra' said: And a group [said]: "wa-man ittaba'anī" (and whoever follows me) is conjoined to the pronoun in "adʿū" (I call), meaning: I and whoever follows me call to God as I call. This is the view of al-Kalbi, who said: It is incumbent upon everyone who follows him to call to what he called to, and to remind [people] with the Qur'an and admonition.

This view is strengthened in many respects:

Ibn al-Anbari said: It is also permissible for the sentence to be complete at His words "to God," and then to begin with His words "upon insight am I and whoever follows me," so that the statement becomes two sentences: in the first he informs that he calls to God, and in the second that he and his followers are upon insight. The two views are mutually implicated, for a man is not truly among his followers until he calls to what he called to and is upon insight.

The view of al-Farra' is better and closer to eloquence and rhetorical excellence.

Since calling to God is the most noble, exalted and virtuous station of the servant, it is not attained except through the knowledge with which one calls and to which one calls. Indeed, perfection in calling requires reaching in knowledge a utmost limit that effort can attain. This suffices for the nobility of knowledge: that its possessor attains this station by it, and "God gives His bounty to whom He wills."

(Benefit)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God upon insight, I and whoever follows me﴾

He informs, exalted is He, that whoever follows the Messenger calls to God, and whoever calls to God upon insight, his following becomes obligatory; this is due to His saying, exalted is He, regarding what He related of the jinn and approved: ﴿O our people, respond to the caller of God and believe in Him﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 31]. Also, whoever calls to God upon insight has called to the truth while knowing it, and calling to the rulings of God is a calling to God, because it is a calling to obedience to Him in what He commanded and forbade. Accordingly, the Companions—may God be pleased with them—followed the Messenger ﷺ, so their following is obligatory when they call to God.

(Section)

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God upon insight, I and whoever follows me﴾

Whether the meaning is "I and whoever follows me call to God upon insight," or the pause is at His saying "I call to God" and then one begins "upon insight am I and whoever follows me," the two views are mutually implicated. He, glorified is He, commanded him to inform that his way is calling to God. So whoever calls to God, exalted is He, is upon the way of His Messenger ﷺ, is upon insight, and is among his followers; and whoever calls to other than that is not upon his way, nor upon insight, nor among his followers.

Calling to God, exalted is He, is the duty of the messengers and their followers, and they are the successors of the messengers among their nations, and people are followers of them. God, glorified is He, commanded His Messenger to convey what was sent down to him, and guaranteed him protection and safeguarding from people. Likewise, those who convey from him from his community have from God's protection and safeguarding according to the measure of their standing by His religion and their conveying it to them. The Prophet ﷺ commanded conveying from him even a single verse, and he invoked blessings upon one who conveys from him even a single hadith. Conveying his Sunnah to the community is more excellent than conveying arrows to the throats of the enemy, because the latter is done by many people, whereas conveying the Sunan is not undertaken except by the heirs of the prophets and their successors among their nations. May God, exalted is He, make us among them by His grace and generosity.

They are as 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, said of them in his sermon, which Ibn Wadah mentioned in his book al-Hawadith wal-Bida': "Praise be to God who has bestowed favour upon the servants by placing in every age, in the interval between messengers, remnants of people of knowledge who call those who have strayed to guidance, bear harm from them with patience, and give life to the blind by the Book of God. How many a slain one of Iblis have they revived, and how many a lost wanderer have they guided! They spent their blood and wealth for the sake of protecting the servants from ruin. How good is their effect upon people, and how evil is people's effect upon them! They are accepted by people in bygone ages and up to this day of ours. Your Lord has not forgotten them: ﴿And your Lord was never forgetful﴾." 

He made their stories a guidance and informed of the goodness of their speech, so do not fall short of them, for they are in an exalted station even if loss befalls them.

And 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, may God be pleased with him, said: "Indeed, for God, at every innovation which seeks to harm Islam, there is a friend of His who defends against it and speaks out its signs. So seize the presence of those occasions and rely upon God."

What suffices in this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ to 'Ali, may God be pleased with him: "That God guides a single man through you is better for you than red camels."

And his saying ﷺ: "Whoever revives something of my Sunnah, he and I will be in Paradise like these two," and he joined his two fingers.

And his saying ﷺ: "Whoever calls to guidance and is followed in it, he will have a reward like the reward of those who follow him until the Day of Resurrection."

When will the worker attain this great virtue and abundant portion through some of his deeds? This is only the bounty of God, which He gives to whom He wills, and God is possessor of great bounty. It is fitting for one who conveys from the Messenger of God ﷺ, whom God, glorified is He, has established in this station, to open his speech with praise of God, extolling Him and acknowledging His oneness and making known His rights over the servants; then with blessings upon the Messenger of God ﷺ, extolling him and praising him; and to close it also with blessings upon him ﷺ, with peace.

[Section: The scholars of the Community are of two kinds]

Since calling to God and conveying from His Messenger is the emblem of His party, the successful ones, and of his followers among all peoples, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Say: This is my way; I call to God upon insight, I and whoever follows me. And glory be to God; and I am not of the polytheists﴾ [Yusuf: 108], and conveying from him consists of conveying his very words and what he brought, and conveying its meanings, the scholars of his community are confined to two categories:

The first: the memorizers of hadith, its critics, and its leaders, who are the imams of mankind and the carriers of Islam, who preserved for the imams the foundations and strongholds of the religion, and protected its wells and watering places from alteration and turbidity, until those for whom the best reward from God had preceded came to those watering places pure from impurities, which opinions had not tainted with change, and drank from them "a spring from which the servants of God drink, making it gush forth abundantly" [al-Insan: 6]. They are those of whom Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal said in his famous preface to his book refuting the zindiqs and the Jahmiyya: "Praise be to God who placed in every age, in the interval between messengers, remnants of people of knowledge who call those who have strayed to guidance, bear harm from them with patience, give life to the dead by the Book of God Most High, and make the blind see by the light of God. How many a slain one of Iblis have they revived, and how many a lost wanderer have they guided! How good is their effect upon people, and how evil is people's effect upon them! They refute from the Book of God the distortion of extremists, the appropriation of falsifiers, and the interpretation of the ignorant, who raised the banners of innovation and let loose the reins of strife. They differ concerning the Book, oppose the Book, and unanimously abandon the Book, speaking about God and about God's Book without knowledge, speaking with the ambiguous part of speech, and deceiving ignorant people with what they confuse for them. So we seek refuge in God from the trial of the misleaders."

The second category: the jurists of Islam, upon whose statements fatwas revolve among mankind, who were singled out for deriving rulings and devoted themselves to fixing the principles of the lawful and the unlawful. They are in the earth like the stars in the sky, by whom the bewildered in darkness are guided. People's need of them is greater than their need of food and drink, and obedience to them is more obligatory upon them than obedience to mothers and fathers by the text of the Book. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿O you who believe, obey God and obey the Messenger and those in authority among you. And if you dispute over anything, refer it to God and the Messenger, if you believe in God and the Last Day. That is better and more excellent in outcome﴾ [al-Nisa': 59]. 'Abd Allah ibn 'Abbas in one of the two reports from him, and Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, al-Hasan al-Basri, Abu al-'Aliya, 'Ata' ibn Abi Rabah, al-Dahhak, and Mujahid in one of the two reports from him, said: "Those in authority" are the scholars; and this is one of the two reports from Imam Ahmad.

Abu Hurayrah and Ibn 'Abbas in the other report, Zayd ibn Aslam, al-Suddi, and Muqatil said: they are the rulers; and this is the second report from Ahmad.

The verification is that rulers are obeyed only when they command in accordance with knowledge; their obedience follows obedience to the scholars, for obedience is only in what is right and what knowledge has made obligatory. Just as obedience to the scholars follows obedience to the Messenger, so obedience to the rulers follows obedience to the scholars. Since the standing of Islam is by the two groups of scholars and rulers, and all people are followers of them, the welfare of the world is by the welfare of these two groups, and its corruption by their corruption, as 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak and other early scholars said: "There are two kinds of people: when they are righteous, people are righteous; and when they are corrupt, people are corrupt." It was asked: "Who are they?" He said: "The kings and the scholars." As 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak said:

I saw sins deaden the hearts, and persistence in them brings about humiliation.
Leaving sins is the life of hearts, and for your soul, disobedience to them is better.
Has anything corrupted religion except kings, and evil rabbis and monks?
This indicates that He did not send a jinn, nor a woman, nor a Bedouin.
